Umbilical cord hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular tumor of the umbilical cord, usually arising near the fetal cord insertion and composed of proliferating blood vessels within edematous or myxoid Wharton's jelly.

Umbilical cord angiomyxoma.description: A benign mesenchymal tumor-like lesion of the umbilical cord characterized by myxoid Wharton's jelly, spindle cells, and variably prominent small blood vessels; it may overlap morphologically with cord hemangioma.

Umbilical cord pseudocyst associated wit.normalized_text: Umbilical cord pseudocyst associated with edema of Wharton's jelly
Umbilical cord pseudocyst associated wit.description: A pseudocyst is a localized accumulation of fluid within degenerated or edematous Wharton's jelly rather than a true epithelial-lined cyst. It can appear as a cord mass on prenatal imaging.

Placental chorioangioma.description: A benign vascular tumor of the placenta composed of capillary-sized vascular channels embedded in fibrous stroma. Large lesions can cause fetal anemia, hydrops, polyhydramnios, or cardiac strain.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells; it is often a hypervascular adrenal mass and can show high signal on T2-weighted MRI.

Adrenal adenoma.description: A common benign tumor of the adrenal cortex, frequently discovered incidentally. Most are nonfunctioning, although some produce cortisol or aldosterone.

Adrenal metastasis.description: Secondary malignant involvement of the adrenal gland, most commonly from lung cancer, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, breast cancer, or gastrointestinal malignancy. Metastases are often indeterminate adrenal masses on imaging.

Adrenal cortical carcinoma.description: A rare malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that may be hormonally active and usually presents as a large heterogeneous adrenal mass with necrosis, hemorrhage, or invasion when advanced.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (multifocal HCC.description: A primary malignant tumor of liver cells, commonly presenting as a dominant hepatic mass with satellite nodules or additional intrahepatic tumors.

Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A variant of hepatocellular carcinoma that often occurs in younger patients without cirrhosis and may appear as a large solitary heterogeneous liver mass, sometimes with satellite lesions.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary cancer of the intrahepatic bile ducts that can form a large liver mass and may produce satellite nodules or multifocal liver involvement.

Hepatic metastases.description: Secondary malignant tumors in the liver originating from a cancer elsewhere in the body; they may present as multiple lesions, including a dominant large metastasis.

Hepatic adenoma.description: A benign hepatocellular tumor that can become large and heterogeneous because of fat, necrosis, or hemorrhage; multiple adenomas can occur in hepatic adenomatosis.

Dominant optic atrophy (OPA1-associated.description: A hereditary optic neuropathy causing slowly progressive bilateral optic nerve degeneration, temporal optic disc pallor, and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON).description: A mitochondrial inherited optic neuropathy that typically produces subacute painless central visual loss followed by bilateral optic atrophy; early fundus findings may include peripapillary telangiectatic vessels and later retinal nerve fiber layer loss.

Multiple sclerosis-associated optic neur.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis-associated optic neuritis with residual optic atrophy
Multiple sclerosis-associated optic neur.description: Inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve can cause optic neuritis and, after prior episodes, residual optic disc pallor and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning. Multiple sclerosis may also cause brain and spinal cord demyelinating lesions.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) or MOG-antibody-associated optic neuritis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: Autoimmune inflammatory disorders that can cause severe, often bilateral optic neuritis with subsequent optic atrophy and retinal nerve fiber layer loss; NMOSD may additionally produce longitudinally extensive myelitis.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7B mutations, resulting in copper accumulation in the liver, cornea, basal ganglia, and other organs.

Aceruloplasminemia.description: A rare autosomal-recessive iron-metabolism disorder caused by ceruloplasmin deficiency, leading to iron deposition in the brain, liver, pancreas, and retina.

Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumu.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by abnormal iron accumulation, particularly in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, often causing dystonia, parkinsonism, and cognitive decline.

Chronic manganese deposition (hepatic en.description: Manganese accumulation can occur in chronic liver dysfunction or portosystemic shunting and may produce bilateral basal ganglia, especially globus pallidus, T1 hyperintensity with neurologic symptoms resembling parkinsonism.

Psoriasis vulgaris.description: A chronic immune-mediated skin disease causing well-demarcated red plaques, often with silvery scale, commonly affecting extensor surfaces such as the elbows and knees.

Dermatitis herpetiformis.description: A chronic intensely itchy blistering skin disorder associated with gluten sensitivity/celiac disease, typically producing grouped papules, vesicles, and excoriations on extensor surfaces.

Rheumatoid nodules.description: Firm subcutaneous nodules that commonly occur over pressure points, especially the elbows, in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and occasionally other inflammatory conditions.

Gouty tophi.description: Deposits of monosodium urate crystals in soft tissues due to longstanding hyperuricemia, often occurring around elbows, ears, fingers, toes, and joints.

Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis.description: Inflammation of the skin caused by exposure to an allergen or irritant, producing redness, papules, swelling, scaling, and sometimes itching or blistering.

Ludwig angina.description: Rapidly progressive cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, often arising from an odontogenic infection and capable of causing airway obstruction.

Angioedema involving the tongue and uppe.normalized_text: Angioedema involving the tongue and upper airway
Angioedema involving the tongue and uppe.description: Acute edema of submucosal tissues, commonly affecting the lips, tongue, floor of mouth, and larynx; it may be allergic, medication-related, or hereditary and can threaten the airway.

Tongue or floor-of-mouth abscess.description: A localized purulent infection within the tongue, sublingual space, or adjacent deep neck spaces that can produce swelling, pain, dysphagia, and airway narrowing.

Lingual hematoma.description: Bleeding into tongue tissues, often after trauma, seizure, anticoagulation, instrumentation, or dental procedures, causing rapid tongue enlargement and possible airway obstruction.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately elevated endogenous insulin secretion.

Sulfonylurea or meglitinide-induced hypo.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin-secretagogue medications, such as sulfonylureas or meglitinides, which stimulate pancreatic insulin release and can mimic insulinoma laboratory findings.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive endogenous insulin secretion, often producing postprandial hypoglycemia but sometimes fasting hypoglycemia as well.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata dise.description: A rare autoimmune disorder in which insulin autoantibodies bind and later release insulin, causing spontaneous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia without exogenous insulin use.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: A hypermobility disorder of the lower false ribs, usually ribs 8 to 10, caused by lax or disrupted interchondral attachments. A rib tip may move beneath or over an adjacent rib and irritate intercostal nerves.

Congenital rib anomaly with bifid or fus.normalized_text: Congenital rib anomaly with bifid or fused rib
Congenital rib anomaly with bifid or fus.description: A developmental variation in which a rib may be partially split, unusually shaped, or connected to an adjacent rib. Such anomalies can be incidentally identified on imaging.

Healed rib fracture with callus formatio.normalized_text: Healed rib fracture with callus formation
Healed rib fracture with callus formatio.description: A prior rib fracture can heal with cortical irregularity, angulation, or callus, altering the contour and spacing of adjacent ribs.

Chest-wall deformity due to rib crowding.normalized_text: Chest-wall deformity due to rib crowding or focal costal cartilage deformity
Chest-wall deformity due to rib crowding.description: A localized chest-wall structural deformity may alter rib spacing or produce prominence of one rib relative to neighboring ribs. It may be congenital, developmental, or post-traumatic.

Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis (colo.description: A benign or secondary condition in which gas-filled cysts develop within the bowel wall, most often in the submucosa or subserosa of the colon.

Colonic lymphangiomatosis / multiple col.description: A benign malformation or proliferation of lymphatic vessels that can produce multiple cystic, submucosal colonic lesions.

Colonic lipomatosis / multiple colonic l.description: Benign fatty submucosal tumors of the colon that may appear as smooth, rounded protrusions into the lumen.

Colonic polyposis syndrome.description: A group of inherited or sporadic disorders characterized by numerous mucosal polyps in the colon, such as adenomatous or hamartomatous polyposis.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent hypereosinophilia, often with dysplastic eosinophil precursors, anemia, abnormal cytogenetics, and possible progression to acute leukemia.

Myelodysplastic syndrome with eosinophil.normalized_text: Myelodysplastic syndrome with eosinophilia and der(1;7)/t(1;7) abnormality
Myelodysplastic syndrome with eosinophil.description: A myelodysplastic neoplasm with ineffective hematopoiesis and dysplastic blood-cell morphology; abnormalities involving chromosomes 1 and 7, including der(1;7), are associated with myeloid neoplasms and can occur with eosinophilia.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangement (for example, FIP1L1-PDGFRA-rearranged neoplasm)
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms driven by rearrangements involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or related genes, commonly presenting with persistent marked eosinophilia and myeloid proliferation.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A diagnosis of persistent unexplained hypereosinophilia with evidence of eosinophil-related organ injury after exclusion of secondary causes and defined clonal hematologic disorders.

Chronic myeloid leukemia or another BCR:.normalized_text: Chronic myeloid leukemia or another BCR::ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm with eosinophilia
Chronic myeloid leukemia or another BCR:.description: Myeloproliferative neoplasms can cause granulocytic proliferation with eosinophilia, basophilia, and circulating immature myeloid cells; chronic myeloid leukemia classically requires demonstration of BCR::ABL1.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.description: A clonal histiocytic neoplasm characterized by proliferation of Langerhans cells, often with eosinophils, which can involve bone, skin, lungs, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys. The histology and immunophenotypic appearance are most compatible with this diagnosis.

Rosai-Dorfman disease.description: A non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder that commonly causes painless lymphadenopathy and may have extranodal involvement, including the kidneys, upper airway, skin, and gastrointestinal tract.

Systemic lymphoma.description: Lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphoid cells that can present with multifocal lymphadenopathy, extranodal abdominal disease, renal infiltration, pulmonary lesions, and FDG uptake on PET.

Erdheim-Chester disease.description: A non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis characterized by systemic infiltration by foamy histiocytes, often affecting long bones, retroperitoneum, kidneys, cardiovascular structures, and the central nervous system.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A life-threatening malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, characterized by high parasitemia, intravascular hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, organ dysfunction, and potentially cerebral, renal, or hepatic complications. The blood smear shows ring-form parasites consistent with P. falciparum, including multiple rings in erythrocytes and an applique form.

Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum mala.description: Malaria due to P. falciparum without clear major-organ complications; however, this patient's profound thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia, and renal impairment make severe malaria more likely.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can cause hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, hepatic enzyme elevation, and renal dysfunction. It can resemble malaria microscopically, although the displayed smear and malaria antigen testing favor P. falciparum.

Dengue fever with severe thrombocytopeni.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection that commonly causes thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, transaminitis, and occasionally hepatic or renal injury. Dengue can coexist with or be confused with malaria in endemic regions, but it does not explain malaria parasites on smear.

Esophageal perforation with acute medias.description: A full-thickness tear or leak in the esophageal wall allowing saliva, gastric contents, and bacteria to enter the mediastinum, causing severe infection and pus formation.

Boerhaave syndrome.description: Spontaneous transmural rupture of the esophagus, classically after forceful vomiting or retching, often causing contamination of the mediastinum and rapidly progressive mediastinitis.

Iatrogenic esophageal perforation.description: An esophageal tear caused by a medical procedure, such as endoscopy, dilation, surgery, intubation, or instrumentation; it can lead to mediastinal infection if not promptly sealed and drained.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disorder that commonly involves intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs and can also involve peripheral lymph nodes and the spleen.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that often presents with painless cervical and mediastinal lymph-node enlargement and may involve the spleen and pleura.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A diverse group of lymphoid malignancies that may cause generalized lymphadenopathy, thoracic nodal enlargement, splenic involvement, and pleural effusions.

Tuberculosis with intrathoracic lymphade.description: Mycobacterial infection that can cause cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, splenic involvement, and chronic lung damage including bronchiectasis.

Hepatic encephalopathy.description: Brain dysfunction caused by liver failure or portosystemic shunting, often producing generalized slowing and frontally predominant triphasic waves on EEG.

Uremic encephalopathy.description: Diffuse cerebral dysfunction due to severe renal failure and accumulation of uremic toxins; EEG may show diffuse slowing and triphasic waves.

Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy.description: Global brain dysfunction caused by metabolic derangements or toxins, including electrolyte abnormalities, hypoglycemia, hypercapnia, sepsis, or medication toxicity. Triphasic waves are a classic EEG finding.

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.description: Persistent seizure activity without prominent convulsive movements, which can present with impaired awareness and generalized periodic or rhythmic EEG discharges. Triphasic waves can sometimes resemble this condition.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.description: A rapidly progressive prion neurodegenerative disorder that may produce periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, typically in the setting of rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus.

Bartholin gland cyst.description: A benign mucus-filled cyst caused by obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct, typically located at the posterolateral vaginal introitus.

Bartholin gland abscess.description: An infected Bartholin duct cyst that forms a painful, inflamed vulvar mass and may contain purulent fluid.

Gartner duct cyst.description: A benign vaginal wall cyst arising from remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, usually located along the anterolateral upper vagina.

Perineal or perianal abscess.description: A localized collection of infected fluid near the anus, perineum, or adjacent soft tissues, often associated with anorectal infection or fistula disease.

Síndrome de Susac.description: Microangiopatía autoinmune poco frecuente que afecta arteriolas del cerebro, retina y oído interno, caracterizada clásicamente por encefalopatía, oclusiones de ramas arteriales retinianas e hipoacusia neurosensorial.

Esclerosis múltiple.description: Enfermedad inflamatoria desmielinizante del sistema nervioso central que produce lesiones en sustancia blanca, con frecuencia periventriculares y del cuerpo calloso, y puede causar síntomas visuales o auditivos.

Vasculitis primaria del sistema nervioso.normalized_text: Vasculitis primaria del sistema nervioso central o vasculitis sistémica con afectación ocular
Vasculitis primaria del sistema nervioso.description: Inflamación de vasos sanguíneos que puede producir infartos cerebrales, isquemia retiniana y, en algunos trastornos sistémicos, compromiso del oído interno.

MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with.normalized_text: MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers), usually due to mitochondrial MT-TK variants
MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with.description: A mitochondrial disorder characterized by myopathy, elevated creatine kinase, epilepsy or myoclonus, and ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy. Severity varies substantially because of mitochondrial heteroplasmy.

MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial e.normalized_text: MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes), often due to MT-TL1 m.3243A>G
MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial e.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disease that can cause variable combinations of myopathy, seizures, elevated CK, encephalopathy, and characteristic mitochondrial abnormalities on muscle biopsy. Some patients present predominantly with adult-onset myopathy rather than classic stroke-like episodes.

POLG-related mitochondrial disease.description: A nuclear-gene mitochondrial disorder caused by POLG variants, ranging from isolated mitochondrial myopathy to epilepsy-associated encephalomyopathy. Muscle biopsy may show ragged-red fibers and respiratory-chain dysfunction.

Autosomal dominant mitochondrial myopath.normalized_text: Autosomal dominant mitochondrial myopathy due to TWNK or another mitochondrial DNA-maintenance gene
Autosomal dominant mitochondrial myopath.description: Dominant disorders of mitochondrial DNA maintenance can produce adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy, axial weakness, elevated CK, and ragged-red fibers. TWNK-related disease commonly includes progressive external ophthalmoplegia but can have broader neurologic manifestations.

Myofibrillar myopathy with rimmed-vacuol.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy with rimmed-vacuole pathology, such as DNAJB6-, DES-, FLNC-, or MYOT-related disease
Myofibrillar myopathy with rimmed-vacuol.description: A group of inherited muscle diseases, often autosomal dominant, causing slowly progressive limb-girdle or axial weakness, camptocormia, and variable CK elevation. Muscle biopsy can show abnormal protein aggregates and rimmed vacuoles that may mimic mitochondrial pathology.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with M.description: An aggressive precursor B-cell neoplasm composed of lymphoblasts, often with Burkitt-like morphology and a MYC gene rearrangement. It may show cytoplasmic vacuolation, immature blast morphology, nuclear TdT positivity, and complex chromosomal abnormalities.

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma driven by MYC rearrangement, classically involving t(8;14), t(2;8), or t(8;22). In leukemic disease, blasts often have intensely basophilic vacuolated cytoplasm.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, B.normalized_text: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, B-cell precursor type
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, B.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-cell lymphoblasts involving bone marrow, blood, lymph nodes, or extranodal sites. Blasts commonly express immature nuclear markers such as TdT and may have chromosomal abnormalities.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma characterized by MYC rearrangement, sometimes accompanied by BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements. It can show blastoid or intermediate morphology and may present with marrow and peripheral-blood involvement.

Peliosis hepatis.description: A rare benign vascular condition characterized by multiple blood-filled cyst-like spaces within the liver, sometimes associated with medications, malignancy, chronic illness, or infection.

Hepatic metastases.description: Secondary malignant deposits in the liver from a cancer arising elsewhere in the body; metastases may be multiple and vary in density or enhancement.

Hepatic lymphoma.description: Liver involvement by lymphoma, either primary hepatic lymphoma or secondary involvement from systemic lymphoma, often producing multiple hypoattenuating liver lesions.

Hepatic sarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation of the liver associated with systemic sarcoidosis; imaging may show numerous small hypodense nodules and hepatomegaly.

Hepatic microabscesses or disseminated h.normalized_text: Hepatic microabscesses or disseminated hepatic infection
Hepatic microabscesses or disseminated h.description: Multiple small liver abscesses may occur with bacterial, fungal, or mycobacterial infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI), likely left anterior descending artery occlusion
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary occlusion, producing ischemic ST-segment and hyperacute T-wave changes in the anterior precordial leads.

De Winter T-wave pattern from proximal l.normalized_text: De Winter T-wave pattern from proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion
De Winter T-wave pattern from proximal l.description: A STEMI-equivalent ECG pattern associated with acute proximal LAD occlusion, typically featuring tall symmetric anterior T waves with upsloping ST depression rather than classic ST elevation.

Hyperkalemia.description: Elevated serum potassium can cause narrow, peaked T waves and may progress to PR prolongation, P-wave flattening, QRS widening, bradyarrhythmias, and sine-wave morphology when severe.

Bronchopulmonary sequestration (left low.normalized_text: Bronchopulmonary sequestration (left lower lobe, likely extralobar)
Bronchopulmonary sequestration (left low.description: A congenital nonfunctioning lung mass that lacks normal bronchial communication and receives anomalous systemic arterial blood supply, usually from the descending aorta.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) with systemic arterial supply (hybrid CPAM-sequestration lesion)
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A congenital cystic lung malformation that may coexist with sequestration and can have an aberrant systemic artery supplying the lesion.

Congenital lobar overinflation (congenit.description: A developmental airway abnormality causing progressive air trapping and overexpansion of one or more lung lobes, often presenting with neonatal respiratory distress.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia or diaph.normalized_text: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia or diaphragmatic eventration with intrathoracic abdominal organ displacement
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia or diaph.description: A congenital diaphragmatic defect or abnormally elevated diaphragm that may permit abdominal contents to enter the thorax or cause apparent lower-lung opacity and reduced lung volume.

Malignant hypertension with hyperplastic.description: Severe, rapidly progressive hypertension can cause concentric smooth-muscle and intimal thickening of small arteries and arterioles, producing an 'onion-skin' appearance and luminal narrowing.

Scleroderma renal crisis.description: A severe vascular complication of systemic sclerosis characterized by abrupt hypertension, acute kidney injury, and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with onion-skin intimal proliferation.

Thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A microvascular occlusive disorder, including hypertensive thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolytic uremic syndrome, or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, that can produce endothelial injury, intimal swelling, and vessel narrowing.

Chronic hypertensive nephrosclerosis.description: Long-standing hypertension causes progressive arteriolar wall thickening and luminal narrowing, usually with hyaline arteriolosclerosis and, when severe, hyperplastic changes.

Chiari I malformation.description: A structural abnormality in which the cerebellar tonsils descend below the foramen magnum, potentially obstructing cerebrospinal fluid flow and compressing the lower brainstem or upper spinal cord.

Basilar invagination (cranial settling).description: Upward displacement of the upper cervical spine, particularly the odontoid process, toward the skull base. It may narrow the foramen magnum and cause compression of the medulla or cervicomedullary junction.

Atlantoaxial instability with ventral ce.normalized_text: Atlantoaxial instability with ventral cervicomedullary compression
Atlantoaxial instability with ventral ce.description: Excessive movement or malalignment between the first and second cervical vertebrae that can allow the odontoid process to compress the spinal cord or lower brainstem.

Infective endocarditis due to an intrins.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis due to an intrinsically vancomycin-resistant Gram-positive organism
Infective endocarditis due to an intrins.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually a cardiac valve, with formation of vegetations and possible valve destruction or regurgitation. The antimicrobial pattern, including marked vancomycin and cephalosporin resistance with relative penicillin/ampicillin susceptibility, can be seen with organisms such as Lactobacillus, Leuconostoc, Weissella, or certain enterococci.

Aortic valve infective endocarditis with.normalized_text: Aortic valve infective endocarditis with severe aortic regurgitation
Aortic valve infective endocarditis with.description: Aortic valve endocarditis is a valve infection that may produce vegetations, leaflet perforation, tissue destruction, and significant aortic regurgitation visible on Doppler echocardiography.

Periannular aortic root abscess complica.normalized_text: Periannular aortic root abscess complicating infective endocarditis
Periannular aortic root abscess complica.description: A periannular abscess is a localized collection of infection extending from an infected valve into surrounding annular or aortic-root tissue. It is a serious complication of infective endocarditis and can cause regurgitation, fistulae, conduction abnormalities, or prosthetic/valve dehiscence.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis.description: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis consists of sterile platelet-fibrin valve vegetations, usually associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease, or severe systemic illness. It can resemble infective endocarditis on echocardiography but generally lacks infectious tissue inflammation and microbiologic evidence.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by thrombus, usually originating from deep venous thrombosis. The CT angiogram shows an intraluminal filling defect in a left pulmonary arterial branch, which is characteristic.

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease.description: Persistent organized thromboembolic material in the pulmonary arteries after prior embolic events; it can lead to chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary artery tumor embolus or pulmon.normalized_text: Pulmonary artery tumor embolus or pulmonary artery sarcoma
Pulmonary artery tumor embolus or pulmon.description: Rare malignant intravascular lesions can create pulmonary arterial filling defects and may mimic thromboembolic pulmonary embolism on contrast CT.

Herpes simplex virus encephalitis.description: Acute viral encephalitis, usually caused by HSV-1, with a characteristic predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insulae, and inferior frontal regions.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid tumor confined to the brain, often showing strong contrast enhancement and surrounding edema; it may occur in immunocompetent or immunocompromised patients.

High-grade glioma, including glioblastom.description: An aggressive primary brain tumor that can produce an enhancing mass with infiltrative edema and may extend through adjacent temporal lobe structures.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic parasitic brain infection, particularly in advanced HIV infection or other severe immunosuppression, commonly presenting with enhancing lesions and surrounding edema.

Severe bacterial sepsis with acute respi.normalized_text: Severe bacterial sepsis with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
Severe bacterial sepsis with acute respi.description: Life-threatening systemic infection causing a dysregulated inflammatory response, organ dysfunction, shock physiology, and severe hypoxemic/hypercapnic respiratory failure.

Legionnaires' disease (severe Legionella.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella species that can produce respiratory failure along with hyponatremia, liver enzyme elevation, renal dysfunction, and rhabdomyolysis.

Hyperinflammatory syndrome / secondary h.description: A severe immune activation syndrome characterized by excessive cytokine release, hyperferritinemia, organ dysfunction, liver injury, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor; it may be triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.

Severe viral pneumonia with rhabdomyolys.normalized_text: Severe viral pneumonia with rhabdomyolysis, such as influenza-associated ARDS
Severe viral pneumonia with rhabdomyolys.description: Severe influenza or another viral lower respiratory infection can cause diffuse lung injury and ARDS, severe hypoxemia, muscle breakdown, liver enzyme elevation, and cardiac biomarker elevation.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phos.normalized_text: Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
Tumor-induced osteomalacia due to a phos.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome caused by a usually benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor that secretes excess FGF23, producing renal phosphate wasting, low phosphate, impaired bone mineralization, and osteomalacia. The pelvic focal uptake/lesion on functional imaging and normalization after resection strongly support this diagnosis.

X-linked hypophosphatemia.description: An inherited FGF23-mediated renal phosphate-wasting disorder, usually caused by PHEX mutations. It typically begins in childhood and causes chronic hypophosphatemia, rickets or osteomalacia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and inappropriately elevated FGF23.

Autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rick.description: A hereditary disorder caused by FGF23 variants resistant to degradation. It leads to increased FGF23 activity, renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, and rickets or osteomalacia; severity can fluctuate with iron status.

Primary hyperparathyroidism with renal p.normalized_text: Primary hyperparathyroidism with renal phosphate wasting
Primary hyperparathyroidism with renal p.description: Excess parathyroid hormone increases renal phosphate excretion and can cause hypophosphatemia. It more commonly causes hypercalcemia and elevated or inappropriately normal PTH, with bone turnover changes in more severe disease.

Infective endocarditis with systemic emb.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, with vegetations that can embolize to the brain, spleen, kidneys, and other organs. Valve destruction may cause significant regurgitation.

Embolic ischemic stroke due to cardiac e.normalized_text: Embolic ischemic stroke due to cardiac embolus
Embolic ischemic stroke due to cardiac e.description: An acute brain infarction caused by embolic occlusion of a cerebral artery, often originating from a cardiac vegetation, thrombus, arrhythmia, or valvular lesion.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis.description: Sterile platelet-fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves, often associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease, or hypercoagulable states; these vegetations can cause recurrent systemic emboli.

Acute valvular regurgitation secondary t.normalized_text: Acute valvular regurgitation secondary to destructive aortic-valve endocarditis
Acute valvular regurgitation secondary t.description: Valve infection can damage or perforate valve leaflets, resulting in severe acute regurgitation and potentially heart failure, while associated vegetations can cause systemic emboli.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia 1 (Sensenbren.description: A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy caused by biallelic variants in ciliary genes such as IFT122. It is characterized by craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, ectodermal abnormalities, skeletal dysplasia with a narrow thorax and short ribs, progressive kidney disease, and variable eye involvement.

IFT122-related short-rib thoracic dyspla.description: A ciliopathy spectrum disorder associated with IFT122 variants, featuring short ribs, a constricted thorax, limb shortening, brachydactyly, renal disease, and variable craniofacial or ectodermal manifestations. Severe forms may cause neonatal respiratory failure, while milder forms overlap with cranioectodermal dysplasia.

Jeune syndrome (asphyxiating thoracic dy.description: An autosomal-recessive skeletal ciliopathy characterized by a narrow, short-rib thorax, respiratory complications, limb shortening, renal disease, and sometimes retinal or other ophthalmologic abnormalities. It is genetically heterogeneous and may overlap clinically with IFT122-related disease.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A renal-skeletal ciliopathy, most often related to genes such as IFT140 or WDR19, characterized by progressive tubulointerstitial kidney disease, retinal or other eye abnormalities, short phalanges, and cone-shaped epiphyses. Thoracic skeletal abnormalities can occur but are generally less prominent than in classic short-rib dysplasia.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive skin findings, including Gottron papules over the knuckles, often with proximal muscle weakness and possible systemic involvement.

Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis.description: A subtype of dermatomyositis with characteristic cutaneous findings but little or no clinically evident muscle weakness; it may be associated with interstitial lung disease or malignancy.

Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis.description: Dermatomyositis associated with an underlying malignancy, particularly in adults; cancer screening is important because the inflammatory skin and muscle disease may occur with or precede tumor detection.

Psoriasis vulgaris.description: A chronic immune-mediated skin disease causing sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with scale, commonly affecting extensor surfaces and sometimes involving the hands and nails.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Childhood osteonecrosis of the femoral head causing fragmentation, flattening, deformity, and possible later hip osteoarthritis. It is usually unilateral but can be bilateral.

Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.description: An inherited skeletal dysplasia characterized by delayed, small, irregular, and fragmented epiphyses, commonly affecting both hips and leading to early degenerative joint disease.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip with.normalized_text: Developmental dysplasia of the hip with residual femoral head deformity
Developmental dysplasia of the hip with.description: Abnormal development of the acetabulum and proximal femur that can cause shallow acetabula, femoral head subluxation, altered femoral head shape, and later osteoarthritis.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck, usually in adolescents, which may be bilateral and can result in deformity or avascular necrosis.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.normalized_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hips
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.description: A chronic inflammatory arthritis of childhood that can involve the hips and cause joint-space narrowing, erosions, growth disturbance, and secondary femoral head deformity.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection of the liver producing a pus-filled cavity; gas-forming organisms can create intralesional gas and an air-fluid level.

Infected simple hepatic cyst.description: A pre-existing benign liver cyst that becomes secondarily infected, potentially producing internal debris, gas, and mass effect.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: A liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica, most commonly located in the right hepatic lobe and capable of becoming very large.

Necrotic hepatic malignancy with superin.description: A primary or metastatic liver tumor may undergo central necrosis and, if infected, can appear as a large cystic lesion with gas.

Alzheimer disease.description: A progressive neurodegenerative dementia characterized by early medial temporal lobe and hippocampal atrophy, often with enlargement of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles.

Hippocampal sclerosis.description: Chronic neuronal loss and gliosis of the hippocampus, most often associated with temporal lobe epilepsy; MRI may show hippocampal atrophy and increased T2/FLAIR signal, usually asymmetric but occasionally bilateral.

Limbic encephalitis.description: An inflammatory, autoimmune, or paraneoplastic disorder affecting the limbic system, commonly producing mesial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling initially, with subsequent hippocampal atrophy in chronic cases.

Frontotemporal dementia, temporal-predom.description: A group of neurodegenerative disorders causing frontal and/or anterior temporal lobe degeneration; temporal-predominant forms can produce marked mesial temporal atrophy and progressive behavioral, language, or semantic impairment.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary jejunal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the small-intestinal mucosa, usually forming infiltrative glands and showing cytokeratin and epithelial membrane antigen expression.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma involving the jejunum
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.description: Colorectal adenocarcinoma can metastasize to or directly involve the small bowel and typically has intestinal glandular morphology with CK20, CDX2, and SATB2 expression.

Metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma involv.normalized_text: Metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma involving the jejunum
Metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma involv.description: Gastric adenocarcinoma may spread to the small intestine and can show infiltrative glandular histology and variable cytokeratin expression.

Germ cell tumor with yolk sac tumor diff.normalized_text: Germ cell tumor with yolk sac tumor differentiation involving the jejunum
Germ cell tumor with yolk sac tumor diff.description: Yolk sac tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor that can rarely involve the gastrointestinal tract and may mimic adenocarcinoma; it commonly expresses AFP, glypican-3, and SALL4.

Active small-bowel gastrointestinal hemo.description: Ongoing bleeding into the small bowel, suggested by a progressively appearing and changing focus of radiotracer activity on serial blood-pool scintigraphy.

Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa and bleeding
Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that can contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing ulceration and significant painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly in younger patients.

Bleeding small-bowel angiodysplasia (art.description: Fragile dilated mucosal blood vessels, often in the small bowel or colon, that can cause intermittent occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia.

Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastroin.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastroin.description: Gastric or duodenal mucosal ulceration, commonly related to Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID exposure, which can erode into a blood vessel and cause major hemorrhage.

Colonic diverticular hemorrhage.description: Bleeding from a colonic diverticulum due to rupture of an adjacent vessel; it can produce sudden, painless, sometimes massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Pulmonary artery aneurysms associated wi.normalized_text: Pulmonary artery aneurysms associated with Behçet disease
Pulmonary artery aneurysms associated wi.description: Behçet disease is a systemic vasculitis that can inflame and weaken pulmonary arterial walls, producing pulmonary artery aneurysms or pseudoaneurysms, sometimes with thrombosis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

Hughes-Stovin syndrome.description: Hughes-Stovin syndrome is a rare vasculitic disorder characterized by pulmonary artery aneurysms and venous thrombosis; it is considered closely related to vascular Behçet disease.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.description: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations are abnormal direct connections between pulmonary arteries and veins, typically appearing as sharply defined enhancing nodules with feeding and draining vessels.

Rasmussen aneurysm.description: A Rasmussen aneurysm is a pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm caused by erosion of an arterial wall adjacent to a chronic tuberculous cavity and may cause life-threatening hemoptysis.

Nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymp.normalized_text: Nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvement
Nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymp.description: A subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma characterized histologically by broad fibrous bands dividing lymphoid tissue into nodules and scattered Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background. Pulmonary involvement can produce masses, nodules, consolidation, or rarely cavitary lesions.

Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis.description: A chronic Aspergillus infection occurring in structurally abnormal lungs, causing one or more thick-walled cavities, progressive upper-lobe infiltrates, pleural thickening, and sometimes fungal balls within cavities.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.description: A hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus, most often in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis, producing central bronchiectasis, mucus impaction, recurrent infiltrates, and sometimes upper-lobe-predominant disease.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with post-tubercu.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection commonly affects the upper lobes and may cause cavitation. Chronic or healed disease can result in fibrosis, volume loss, and traction bronchiectasis.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary d.description: Chronic infection with organisms such as Mycobacterium avium complex can cause nodular bronchiectatic disease or fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease, especially in patients with underlying lung abnormalities.

Natalizumab-associated progressive multi.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus (JCPyV), particularly in patients receiving natalizumab or other immunosuppressive therapies. JCPyV noncoding control region rearrangements are associated with neurotropic viral variants found in PML.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute or subacute recurrence of inflammatory demyelinating disease in the central nervous system. Natalizumab is commonly used to treat relapsing multiple sclerosis, so a new neurologic event in this setting may represent either an MS relapse or PML.

JC polyomavirus granule cell neuronopath.normalized_text: JC polyomavirus granule cell neuronopathy (JCPyV GCN)
JC polyomavirus granule cell neuronopath.description: A rare JCPyV-associated neurologic disorder in which the virus infects cerebellar granule neurons, producing progressive cerebellar atrophy and ataxia. It can occur in immunosuppressed patients, including those receiving natalizumab.

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease).description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the heart, kidneys, nervous system, and skin. Cardiac involvement commonly produces concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy and characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions ('zebra bodies') on electron microscopy.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric, with possible diastolic dysfunction, outflow obstruction, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death risk.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal/autophagy-related disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It can cause severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and intellectual disability, particularly in affected males.

Hydronephrosis due to urinary tract obst.normalized_text: Hydronephrosis due to urinary tract obstruction
Hydronephrosis due to urinary tract obst.description: Dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces caused by impaired urine drainage, commonly from a ureteral stone, stricture, mass, or prostatic obstruction.

Pyonephrosis.description: Infected hydronephrosis, in which pus accumulates in an obstructed renal collecting system; this is a urologic emergency.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis.description: A severe gas-forming bacterial infection of the kidney, usually occurring in patients with diabetes or urinary obstruction; ultrasound may show echogenic foci with reverberation or dirty acoustic shadowing.

Herpes zoster (shingles), likely involvi.normalized_text: Herpes zoster (shingles), likely involving the trigeminal and auricular distribution
Herpes zoster (shingles), likely involvi.description: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus causing painful grouped vesicles and bullae on an erythematous base, usually in a unilateral dermatomal pattern.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster otic.description: Varicella-zoster virus infection involving the ear, sometimes with facial nerve involvement; it produces painful vesicles on the auricle, ear canal, and nearby face.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, characterized by fragile blisters, erosions, crusting, and sometimes honey-colored exudate.

Herpes simplex virus infection (extensiv.normalized_text: Herpes simplex virus infection (extensive facial herpes simplex)
Herpes simplex virus infection (extensiv.description: Herpes simplex virus can cause clusters of painful vesicles that rupture to form erosions and crusts; severe or extensive disease is more likely in immunocompromised individuals.

Bullous pemphigoid.description: An autoimmune blistering disorder, usually in older adults, causing tense blisters on inflamed or normal-appearing skin and often associated with itching.

Renal hydatid cyst (renal echinococcosis.description: A rare parasitic infection caused by Echinococcus that can form a multiloculated cyst in the kidney, often containing daughter cysts.

Complex renal cyst (Bosniak III or IV cy.normalized_text: Complex renal cyst (Bosniak III or IV cystic renal lesion)
Complex renal cyst (Bosniak III or IV cy.description: A complex kidney cyst with internal septations, thick walls, calcification, or solid components; higher Bosniak categories may represent malignancy.

Cystic renal cell carcinoma.description: A malignant kidney tumor that may appear predominantly cystic, often with thick septa, mural nodules, enhancing solid portions, or irregular walls on imaging.

Renal abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the kidney that produces a complex fluid collection, sometimes with internal debris, septations, or a thick irregular wall.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia wit.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia wit.description: A rapidly progressive, often fulminant bloodstream infection caused by Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a dog- and cat-associated gram-negative rod. It can cause septic shock, DIC, purpura fulminans, acral ischemia/necrosis, multiorgan failure, and marked hepatic injury.

Purpura fulminans due to severe bacteria.normalized_text: Purpura fulminans due to severe bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Purpura fulminans due to severe bacteria.description: Purpura fulminans is a catastrophic thrombotic skin syndrome caused by severe depletion or dysfunction of natural anticoagulant pathways during sepsis-associated DIC. It produces rapidly spreading purpura, skin necrosis, distal ischemia, bleeding, and multiorgan failure.

Meningococcal septicemia with meningococ.normalized_text: Meningococcal septicemia with meningococcal purpura fulminans
Meningococcal septicemia with meningococ.description: Fulminant Neisseria meningitidis bloodstream infection can cause abrupt sepsis, petechiae/purpura, DIC, adrenal injury, shock, and multiorgan failure. The rash may progress to extensive purpura fulminans and limb ischemia.

Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with necrot.normalized_text: Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with necrotizing skin infection and DIC
Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with necrot.description: Vibrio vulnificus is a gram-negative marine bacterium that can cause fulminant septicemia, especially in people with liver disease or iron overload. It commonly produces painful hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymoses, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, DIC, shock, renal failure, and hepatic dysfunction.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic ac.normalized_text: Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke
Left atrial myxoma with cardioembolic ac.description: A left atrial myxoma is a benign primary cardiac tumor, usually attached to the interatrial septum. Fragments of tumor or associated thrombus can embolize to cerebral arteries and cause acute ischemic stroke.

Acute embolic ischemic stroke due to lef.normalized_text: Acute embolic ischemic stroke due to left middle cerebral artery occlusion
Acute embolic ischemic stroke due to lef.description: An acute ischemic stroke occurs when arterial blood flow to brain tissue is blocked. Emboli commonly occlude branches of the middle cerebral artery and produce cortical diffusion restriction on MRI.

Left atrial thrombus with cerebral embol.normalized_text: Left atrial thrombus with cerebral embolization
Left atrial thrombus with cerebral embol.description: A thrombus in the left atrium or left atrial appendage can embolize into the systemic circulation and obstruct a cerebral artery, causing ischemic stroke. It is often associated with atrial fibrillation, atrial enlargement, or impaired cardiac function.

Infective endocarditis with septic cereb.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic cerebral embolus
Infective endocarditis with septic cereb.description: Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve. Vegetations can embolize to the brain and cause ischemic infarction or hemorrhagic complications.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant adenocarcinoma arising from the distal common bile duct, commonly causing progressive extrahepatic biliary obstruction and jaundice. Histology typically shows infiltrating malignant glands in dense desmoplastic stroma.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: An aggressive gland-forming carcinoma of pancreatic ducts, most often arising in the pancreatic head and producing obstruction of the common bile duct, jaundice, elevated CA 19-9, and sometimes pancreatic enzyme elevation.

Ampullary adenocarcinoma.description: A carcinoma arising from the ampulla of Vater, where the distal common bile duct and pancreatic duct enter the duodenum. It can cause early biliary obstruction and may resemble distal cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic-head cancer on imaging.

Gallbladder carcinoma with biliary tract.normalized_text: Gallbladder carcinoma with biliary tract invasion
Gallbladder carcinoma with biliary tract.description: A malignancy arising from the gallbladder epithelium that can invade the hepatic hilum, common hepatic duct, or distal bile duct and cause obstructive jaundice. Most are adenocarcinomas and may elevate CA 19-9.

Benign distal biliary obstruction from c.normalized_text: Benign distal biliary obstruction from choledocholithiasis with inflammatory stricture
Benign distal biliary obstruction from c.description: A common bile duct stone or inflammatory narrowing can obstruct bile flow, causing jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. CA 19-9 can rise transiently in benign cholestasis, although malignant cytology or tissue would argue against this diagnosis.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, most often caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone.

Cholelithiasis with cystic duct obstruct.description: Gallstones within the gallbladder or cystic duct that may cause intermittent or persistent obstruction and biliary colic.

Gallbladder adenomyomatosis.description: A benign hyperplastic gallbladder-wall condition characterized by wall thickening and intramural diverticula known as Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses.

Gallbladder carcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the gallbladder that can present as focal or diffuse wall thickening, a polypoid mass, or invasion of adjacent liver tissue.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (tibial tubercl.description: An overuse traction injury of the tibial tubercle growth area, most often occurring in physically active adolescents during growth spurts.

Tibial tubercle avulsion fracture.description: An acute fracture caused by forceful contraction of the quadriceps tendon, pulling a fragment from the tibial tubercle; usually occurs in adolescents during jumping or sprinting.

Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome.description: A traction apophysitis involving the inferior pole of the patella, causing anterior knee pain in active children and adolescents.

Lichen planopilaris.description: A lymphocyte-mediated cicatricial alopecia in which inflammation targets the upper portion of hair follicles, causing perifollicular scale, progressive follicular destruction, and permanent scarring hair loss.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia together with widespread follicular keratotic or lichenoid papules, often with loss of body hair in axillary or pubic areas.

Follicular lichen planus.description: A follicular form of lichen planus that produces small keratotic follicular papules and may coexist with lichen planopilaris when the scalp follicles become involved.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common benign disorder of follicular keratinization causing small rough follicular papules, usually on the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, and sometimes trunk.

Livedoid vasculopathy.description: A thrombotic disorder of small dermal blood vessels causing recurrent, painful ulcers around the ankles and feet that heal with white, stellate, scar-like areas known as atrophie blanche. Histology often shows hyalinized or thrombosed superficial dermal vessels with little primary inflammation.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa.description: A skin-limited necrotizing vasculitis involving small-to-medium arteries, usually on the lower legs. It can cause tender nodules, livedo-like discoloration, purpura, and ulcers near the ankles.

Venous stasis ulcer due to chronic venou.normalized_text: Venous stasis ulcer due to chronic venous insufficiency
Venous stasis ulcer due to chronic venou.description: Chronic venous hypertension causes edema, brown hemosiderin pigmentation, stasis dermatitis, and ulcers, classically in the gaiter region around the medial ankle.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.description: A rare malignant vascular tumor composed of epithelioid endothelial cells, often showing cytoplasmic vacuoles or primitive vascular lumina and positivity for endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG, FLI1, and CD34.

Epithelioid angiosarcoma.description: An aggressive high-grade malignant endothelial tumor that can form solid sheets of pleomorphic epithelioid cells with only subtle vascular-channel formation. It commonly expresses CD31, ERG, FLI1, and sometimes cytokeratin.

Metastatic poorly differentiated carcino.description: A metastatic epithelial malignancy can produce sheets or nests of atypical epithelioid cells and may mimic vascular tumors, particularly when the tumor is poorly differentiated or has clear-cell or signet-ring-like features.

Malignant melanoma, epithelioid type.description: An aggressive melanocytic malignancy that may consist of pleomorphic epithelioid cells and can histologically resemble carcinoma or sarcoma. Typical immunostains include SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor showing acinar differentiation and production of digestive enzymes. It is often a large, well-circumscribed heterogeneous pancreatic mass with areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasm, usually occurring in young women, that commonly forms a large encapsulated solid and cystic mass with hemorrhagic degeneration.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm derived from pancreatic endocrine cells. Larger tumors may be nonfunctioning, well-defined, hypervascular, and can undergo hemorrhage or necrosis.

Pancreatoblastoma.description: A rare malignant embryonal pancreatic tumor with acinar differentiation, most often occurring in infants and young children. Histology may include acinar structures and characteristic squamoid corpuscles.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from ductal epithelium. It typically causes an infiltrative hypovascular mass with desmoplastic stroma and gland-forming malignant cells.

Segmental (localized) Darier disease.description: A mosaic form of Darier disease, an inherited keratinization disorder characterized by keratotic crusted papules and plaques with acantholysis and dyskeratosis on biopsy. Segmental disease is limited to one body region or side.

Acantholytic dyskeratotic epidermal nevu.description: A localized epidermal nevus with Darier-like microscopic changes, including acantholysis and dyskeratosis. It often follows a mosaic or segmental distribution and may clinically resemble localized Darier disease.

Hailey-Hailey disease.description: A genetic acantholytic disorder causing recurrent painful erosions, fissures, and macerated plaques in intertriginous regions such as the axillae, groin, and neck.

Hidradenitis suppurativa.description: A chronic inflammatory disorder of hair follicles in flexural regions that causes recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, draining sinus tracts, scarring, and comedone-like openings.

Pelvic chondrosarcoma.description: A malignant cartilage-producing bone tumor, commonly arising in the pelvis in adults. It typically appears as a large lobulated expansile lytic lesion with characteristic chondroid matrix calcification and possible soft-tissue extension.

Low-grade conventional chondrosarcoma.description: A relatively slow-growing conventional cartilage malignancy that may initially have limited symptoms but can progressively enlarge, expand bone, and form a lobulated pelvic mass with chondroid calcification.

Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma.description: A high-grade malignant tumor in which a conventional cartilaginous tumor coexists with an aggressive non-cartilaginous sarcoma. It often occurs in the pelvis and can produce a large destructive mass.

Enchondroma or atypical cartilaginous tu.description: A benign or locally aggressive cartilage-forming bone lesion that can contain rings-and-arcs calcification. In the pelvis, large lesions with cortical destruction are more concerning for chondrosarcoma than for a benign enchondroma.

Classical anti-GAD stiff-person syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and proximal limb stiffness, painful spasms, exaggerated startle responses, and continuous motor-unit activity caused by impaired GABAergic inhibition. High-titer glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies strongly support this diagnosis.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum disorder featuring rigidity, muscle spasms, myoclonus, brainstem dysfunction, autonomic instability, and encephalopathy. It is often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, although anti-GAD antibodies can occur.

Paraneoplastic stiff-person syndrome.description: A stiff-person-spectrum disorder associated with an underlying malignancy, commonly breast cancer or small-cell lung cancer, and frequently associated with amphiphysin antibodies. It may present with prominent stiffness and spasms, often involving the trunk and limbs.

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) with scalp necrosis
Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, usually in older adults, that can involve the superficial temporal and occipital arteries and cause scalp ischemia, ulceration, or necrosis.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, causing arterial stenosis or occlusion and ischemic complications. Severe carotid or subclavian involvement can rarely contribute to scalp ischemia.

Atherosclerotic carotid or great-vessel.normalized_text: Atherosclerotic carotid or great-vessel occlusive disease
Atherosclerotic carotid or great-vessel.description: Atherosclerosis can narrow or block major arteries supplying the head and neck. Severe multivessel disease may cause tissue ischemia and, rarely, scalp ulceration or necrosis.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause skin nodules, ulcers, livedo reticularis, neuropathy, and ischemic tissue injury; scalp involvement is uncommon.

Cold agglutinin disease (cold autoimmune.normalized_text: Cold agglutinin disease (cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia)
Cold agglutinin disease (cold autoimmune.description: An autoimmune hemolytic anemia caused by cold-reactive IgM antibodies that agglutinate red blood cells and can activate complement-mediated hemolysis.

Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria.description: A rare complement-mediated autoimmune hemolytic anemia caused by a biphasic cold-reacting antibody, typically producing episodic intravascular hemolysis after cold exposure.

Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.description: An autoimmune disorder in which warm-reactive IgG antibodies bind red blood cells, leading predominantly to extravascular hemolysis and anemia.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis that commonly presents as annular plaques and histologically shows palisading granulomatous inflammation surrounding altered collagen (necrobiotic collagen), often with mucin.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder, often associated with diabetes mellitus, characterized by yellow-brown atrophic plaques with erythematous or violaceous borders; biopsy shows necrobiotic collagen with granulomatous inflammation.

Rheumatoid nodule.description: A firm subcutaneous inflammatory nodule seen most often in patients with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, especially over pressure points. Histology classically demonstrates central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes and chronic inflammation.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B;.description: An imprinting-related disorder causing renal resistance to parathyroid hormone, usually due to abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH despite preserved kidney function.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A;.normalized_text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A; maternally inherited GNAS inactivating variant)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A;.description: A disorder of PTH resistance caused by an inactivating GNAS variant inherited from the mother. It typically causes hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH, often with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features.

Primary hypoparathyroidism.description: Deficient PTH secretion, commonly from autoimmune, genetic, postsurgical, or infiltrative causes, resulting in hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.

Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.description: Reduced phosphate excretion in chronic kidney disease can cause hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and compensatory elevation of PTH.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, usually in an immunocompromised host, causing reticuloendothelial involvement of the liver, spleen, bone marrow, lungs, and occasionally kidneys. Tissue commonly shows granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.

Disseminated candidiasis with hepatosple.description: Invasive Candida infection in an immunocompromised or oncologic patient that can disseminate hematogenously and produce microabscesses in the liver and spleen, persistent cytopenias, cholestatic liver injury, renal dysfunction, and fungal elements on tissue stains.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Systemic infection with Cryptococcus species, usually in patients with impaired cellular immunity. It may involve the lungs, bloodstream, central nervous system, liver, kidneys, and bone marrow; tissue may show yeast forms on fungal stains.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), potentially triggered by disseminated fungal infection
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome triggered by infections, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. It causes cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy with hypofibrinogenemia, renal injury, and progressive multiorgan failure; disseminated histoplasmosis is a recognized trigger.

Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwis.normalized_text: Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwise specified
Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwis.description: A rare sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor composed of steroid-producing cells with abundant clear or vacuolated cytoplasm. It may secrete androgens or other steroid hormones, although some cases are nonfunctioning.

Ovarian Leydig cell tumor.description: A usually benign androgen-producing ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor, often small and unilateral. Histologically, it is composed of polygonal steroid cells and may contain Reinke crystals.

Ovarian clear cell carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial ovarian tumor characterized by clear cells, hobnail cells, and tubulocystic or solid growth patterns. It is frequently associated with endometriosis and is typically larger or more complex than benign steroid-cell tumors.

Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcino.normalized_text: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma involving the ovary
Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcino.description: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma can metastasize to the ovary and may resemble a primary ovarian clear-cell or steroid-cell tumor because of its clear cytoplasm and rich vascular network.

Familial syringomyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, here involving the cervical cord. The pedigree suggests an autosomal-recessive familial form because an affected child was born to unaffected related parents.

Syringomyelia associated with Chiari I m.normalized_text: Syringomyelia associated with Chiari I malformation
Syringomyelia associated with Chiari I m.description: Syringomyelia commonly occurs when Chiari I malformation obstructs cerebrospinal-fluid flow at the craniocervical junction, producing a cervical spinal cord syrinx.

Syringohydromyelia due to a congenital s.normalized_text: Syringohydromyelia due to a congenital spinal cord developmental abnormality
Syringohydromyelia due to a congenital s.description: Syringohydromyelia is dilation of the spinal cord central canal and/or formation of a syrinx, which may result from congenital abnormalities affecting cerebrospinal-fluid circulation or spinal cord development.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related infl.description: An inflammatory reaction to amyloid-beta deposited in cortical and leptomeningeal cerebral vessels, typically causing asymmetric white-matter edema, small ischemic lesions, and lobar microhemorrhages.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: A rare vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord that can cause multifocal ischemic infarcts, inflammatory white-matter abnormalities, and intracranial hemorrhage.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, often associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, eclampsia, immunosuppressive therapy, or systemic illness; hemorrhage and small infarcts can occur in severe cases.

Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke with.normalized_text: Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke with hemorrhagic transformation
Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke with.description: Multiple emboli from a cardiac or arterial source can produce scattered acute infarcts in different vascular territories; infarcts may develop petechial hemorrhage.

Intramedullary spinal cord sarcoidosis (.description: A granulomatous inflammatory manifestation of sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord, often producing an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion and noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.

Intramedullary spinal tuberculoma.description: A focal granulomatous infection of the spinal cord caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It can appear as an enhancing intramedullary lesion and may show granulomas and giant cells on biopsy, often with caseous necrosis.

Fungal granuloma of the spinal cord.normalized_text: Fungal granuloma of the spinal cord
Fungal granuloma of the spinal cord.description: A fungal infection, such as cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, or aspergillosis, can rarely produce an intramedullary granulomatous mass with inflammatory cells and giant cells.

Idiopathic granulomatous myelitis.description: A rare inflammatory disorder characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the spinal cord after infectious, systemic sarcoid, autoimmune, and neoplastic causes have been excluded.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis.description: Fungal lung infection caused by Cryptococcus species, often producing nodules, consolidation, cavitation, or mass-like lesions; tissue may show yeast organisms with clear halos and granulomatous or macrophage-rich inflammation.

Pulmonary nocardiosis.description: An opportunistic bacterial infection caused by Nocardia species that can cause necrotizing pneumonia, cavitary consolidation, nodules, and abscesses, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Pulmonary abscess / necrotizing bacteria.description: A localized destructive bacterial lung infection causing pus-filled cavitation within an area of consolidation; common pathogens include anaerobes, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and gram-negative organisms.

Pulmonary Rhodococcus equi infection.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Rhodococcus equi that may produce cavitary pneumonia and is characteristically associated with foamy macrophages on tissue examination, especially in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides infecti.description: Intestinal infection caused by the large roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. Adult female worms have a thick cuticle and prominent reproductive tubes containing eggs, consistent with the histologic appearance shown.

Toxocariasis (Toxocara species infection.description: A zoonotic roundworm infection acquired from dogs or cats. Humans usually harbor migrating larvae rather than adult egg-producing worms, causing visceral or ocular larva migrans.

Enterobiasis (Enterobius vermicularis, p.description: A common intestinal nematode infection in which adult pinworms inhabit the colon and females deposit eggs around the anus, often causing nocturnal itching.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early postural instability, axial parkinsonism, slowing of vertical saccades, and eventually vertical supranuclear gaze palsy. MRI may show marked midbrain atrophy with the 'hummingbird' or 'penguin' sign.

Midbrain stroke causing vertical gaze pa.normalized_text: Midbrain stroke causing vertical gaze palsy
Midbrain stroke causing vertical gaze pa.description: An ischemic or hemorrhagic lesion involving the rostral midbrain, riMLF, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, or posterior commissure can cause acute vertical gaze paresis or palsy.

Dorsal midbrain syndrome (Parinaud syndr.description: A syndrome caused by dysfunction of the dorsal midbrain, commonly from pineal-region lesions, hydrocephalus, multiple sclerosis, or infarction. It classically causes impaired upward gaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and light-near dissociation of the pupils.

Parkinson disease with advanced ocular-m.normalized_text: Parkinson disease with advanced ocular-motor dysfunction
Parkinson disease with advanced ocular-m.description: Parkinson disease is a synucleinopathy causing bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and hypomimia. Mild slowing of vertical saccades may occur, but an early severe vertical gaze palsy is more suggestive of PSP.

Cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans.normalized_text: Cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii infection)
Cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans.description: An invasive fungal infection caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast. It commonly causes meningitis or meningoencephalitis, especially in people with impaired cellular immunity, although C. gattii can affect immunocompetent individuals.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: Central nervous system infection by Cryptococcus, usually due to C. neoformans or C. gattii, characterized by yeast in cerebrospinal fluid and potentially causing elevated intracranial pressure.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Widespread Cryptococcus infection involving blood, lungs, skin, central nervous system, or other organs, most often in patients with advanced HIV infection, transplant-related immunosuppression, malignancy, or corticosteroid exposure.

Histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, usually acquired by inhaling spores. Disseminated disease may occur in immunocompromised patients, but the organism is typically a small intracellular yeast without the prominent capsule seen here.
