Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central.description: A demyelinating injury of the central pons, most often associated with rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia or other major osmotic shifts. MRI commonly shows central pontine T2 hyperintensity with diffusion restriction.

Acute pontine ischemic infarction.description: An acute stroke affecting the pons, usually due to occlusion of small perforating branches of the basilar artery or basilar artery disease. Acute infarcts typically demonstrate restricted diffusion on MRI.

Brainstem encephalitis.description: Inflammation of the brainstem caused by infection, autoimmune disease, or paraneoplastic processes. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity in the pons and can occasionally show diffusion abnormalities.

Pontine glioma or infiltrative brainstem.normalized_text: Pontine glioma or infiltrative brainstem tumor
Pontine glioma or infiltrative brainstem.description: A tumor arising within or infiltrating the brainstem, which may produce pontine enlargement and T2 hyperintensity. In adults, focal glioma and other infiltrative neoplasms are possible considerations.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Life-threatening malaria caused by P. falciparum, characterized by high-grade parasitemia, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, organ dysfunction, and potential cerebral involvement. Multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and very high parasite density strongly support this diagnosis.

Congenital or neonatal Plasmodium falcip.normalized_text: Congenital or neonatal Plasmodium falciparum malaria
Congenital or neonatal Plasmodium falcip.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery, most often presenting in early infancy with anemia, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and parasites on peripheral blood smear. P. falciparum can cause severe disease with high parasitemia in neonates.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoal infection caused by Babesia species that produces hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and ring forms on blood smear. Severe disease can occur with high parasite burdens, particularly in immunocompromised or asplenic patients.

Severe malaria-associated disseminated i.description: A consumptive coagulopathy that can complicate severe malaria and other overwhelming infections, causing thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated D-dimer, and bleeding or thrombosis risk.

Metastatic uterine leiomyosarcoma.description: An aggressive smooth-muscle cancer of the uterus that commonly spreads hematogenously to the lungs and may also involve the liver and pelvis.

Benign metastasizing leiomyoma.description: A rare condition in which histologically benign uterine smooth-muscle tumors, usually in women with prior uterine leiomyomas or uterine surgery, appear as slow-growing pulmonary nodules and occasionally occur at extrapulmonary sites.

Metastatic endometrial stromal sarcoma.description: A uterine mesenchymal malignancy that can recur or metastasize years after initial treatment, particularly to the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, and liver.

Metastatic epithelial malignancy of pelv.normalized_text: Metastatic epithelial malignancy of pelvic origin, such as ovarian or endometrial carcinoma
Metastatic epithelial malignancy of pelv.description: A gynecologic cancer can disseminate to the liver and lungs, with a pelvic mass potentially representing the primary tumor or recurrent disease.

Graves disease.description: An autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism characterized by diffuse thyroid enlargement, marked increased thyroid blood flow ("thyroid inferno"), follicular hyperplasia with papillary infoldings, scalloped colloid, and variable lymphocytic infiltration.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: A potentially life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis, often due to Graves disease, in which intracellular potassium shifting produces profound hypokalemia and episodic muscle weakness or paralysis.

Hashimoto thyroiditis with transient thy.description: Autoimmune thyroiditis with lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of thyroid follicles; a transient hyperthyroid phase can occur when stored thyroid hormone is released from damaged follicles.

Bifid uvula.description: A congenital split or duplication of the uvula, sometimes occurring alone and sometimes associated with a submucous cleft palate.

Submucous cleft palate.description: A congenital palatal cleft covered by intact mucosa; a bifid uvula can be a visible marker. Some affected people have velopharyngeal insufficiency or speech and swallowing problems.

Uvular edema (uvulitis or Quincke edema).description: Acute swelling of the uvula caused by infection, irritation, trauma, medication reaction, or allergy; potentially urgent if it causes breathing or swallowing impairment.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal, often caused by degenerative disc bulging, facet joint arthritis, and ligament thickening; the MRI appearance suggests marked central canal narrowing in the lower lumbar spine.

Lumbar degenerative disc disease.description: Age- or wear-related degeneration of lumbar intervertebral discs, with disc dehydration, loss of disc height, and broad-based disc bulging.

Lumbar disc herniation, likely at L4-L5.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation, likely at L4-L5
Lumbar disc herniation, likely at L4-L5.description: Protrusion or extrusion of disc material into the spinal canal that can compress the thecal sac or nerve roots; the image suggests a posterior lower-lumbar disc protrusion contributing to canal narrowing.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular dysplasia characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and visceral arteriovenous malformations, especially in the lungs, brain, liver, and gastrointestinal tract.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation wit.normalized_text: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation with paradoxical cerebral embolization
Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation wit.description: A direct abnormal connection between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that creates a right-to-left shunt, allowing thrombi, air, or septic material to bypass the pulmonary capillary filter and reach the cerebral circulation.

Cerebral arteriovenous malformation (bra.description: A congenital high-flow vascular lesion consisting of direct artery-to-vein connections without an intervening capillary bed. Brain AVMs can cause intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, or ischemic complications.

Cerebral septic emboli or brain abscess.normalized_text: Cerebral septic emboli or brain abscess related to a pulmonary right-to-left shunt
Cerebral septic emboli or brain abscess.description: Patients with pulmonary AVMs are predisposed to cerebral septic emboli and brain abscess because bacteria can bypass normal pulmonary capillary filtration through the right-to-left shunt.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and the lungs.

Tuberculosis.description: A mycobacterial infection that can cause granulomatous inflammation and thoracic lymphadenopathy, usually with caseating necrosis and often upper-lung involvement.

Lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that may present with intensely FDG-avid mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy; granulomatous reactions can occasionally occur adjacent to lymphoma.

Fungal granulomatous infection, such as.normalized_text: Fungal granulomatous infection, such as histoplasmosis
Fungal granulomatous infection, such as.description: Certain fungal infections can produce granulomas and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy, sometimes mimicking sarcoidosis on PET and CT imaging.

Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (Albers.description: An inherited osteoclast dysfunction disorder causing failure of normal bone resorption, diffuse osteosclerosis, very high bone mineral density, and structurally abnormal but potentially brittle bone.

Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase.normalized_text: Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase II deficiency
Osteopetrosis due to carbonic anhydrase.description: A recessive form of osteopetrosis caused by impaired osteoclast acidification, usually associated with osteosclerosis, cerebral calcification, renal tubular acidosis, and developmental impairment.

High-bone-mass syndrome due to LRP5 gain.normalized_text: High-bone-mass syndrome due to LRP5 gain-of-function mutation
High-bone-mass syndrome due to LRP5 gain.description: A genetic high-bone-mass disorder caused by increased Wnt signaling and enhanced bone formation, producing very high DXA values and generalized osteosclerosis, often without marrow failure.

Skeletal fluorosis.description: A metabolic bone disorder caused by chronic excessive fluoride exposure, leading to diffuse osteosclerosis, increased bone density, calcification of ligaments, and sometimes bone pain or stiffness.

Germinoma supraselar/intracraneal con af.description: Un tumor primario de células germinales del sistema nervioso central que suele surgir en la región pineal o suprasellar y puede afectar al hipotálamo y al tallo pituitario, causando diabetes insípida y deficiencias hormonales de la hipófisis anterior. Pueden producirse lesiones multifocales que aumentan la línea media.

Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso ce.normalized_text: Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso central que afecta al hipotálamo y al tallo hipofisario
Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso ce.description: El linfoma primario del SNC es un tumor linfoide maligno que puede presentarse con lesiones cerebrales fuertemente potenciadas y, al afectar la región hipotalámica-hipofisaria, puede producir diabetes insípida central e hipopituitarismo.

Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al eje hipot.normalized_text: Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al eje hipotalámico-hipófisis
Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al eje hipot.description: La neurosarcoidosis es una inflamación granulomatosa del sistema nervioso que puede infiltrarse en el hipotálamo, el tallo hipofisario, las meninges y las vías ópticas. Puede causar diabetes insípida central, hiperprolactinemia y múltiples deficiencias anterohipófisis.

Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans c.normalized_text: Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans con afectación hipotalámica-hipofisaria
Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans c.description: La histiocitosis de células de Langerhan es un trastorno histiocítico clonal que puede infiltrarse en el tallo hipofisario y el hipotálamo. La diabetes insípida central es una presentación endocrina común, y puede desarrollarse disfunción hipofisaria anterior.

Cor triatriatum sinister.description: A rare congenital cardiac anomaly in which a fibromuscular membrane divides the left atrium into a pulmonary venous chamber and a distal chamber connected to the mitral valve, causing variable obstruction to pulmonary venous flow.

Supramitral ring.description: A congenital membrane located immediately above the mitral valve that obstructs inflow from the left atrium to the left ventricle and can resemble congenital mitral stenosis.

Mitral stenosis.description: Narrowing of the mitral valve, most commonly rheumatic in origin, leading to impaired left atrial emptying, left atrial enlargement, and pulmonary venous congestion.

Left atrial myxoma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising from the interatrial septum, that can intermittently obstruct the mitral valve and produce symptoms similar to mitral stenosis.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation, especially in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile disease causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, weakness, and respiratory failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A disorder characterized by abnormal thickening of the heart muscle, which may be genetic, metabolic, or secondary to conditions such as Pompe disease. In infants it can cause cardiomegaly, heart failure, and poor feeding.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal/autophagy-related disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and intellectual disability, usually with a later childhood or adolescent presentation than classic infantile Pompe disease.

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.description: A group of genetic disorders affecting mitochondrial energy production that can present in infancy with hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, lactic acidosis, and multisystem disease.

B-lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (precu.description: An aggressive neoplasm of immature B-cell lymphoblasts that may present as extranodal soft-tissue, renal, nodal, or marrow disease. It is termed leukemia when there is substantial bone-marrow or peripheral-blood involvement.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that frequently involves extranodal organs, particularly the abdomen, kidneys, bone marrow, and central nervous system.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: The most common aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma, often presenting with nodal or extranodal masses and systemic inflammation; renal, soft-tissue, and marrow involvement may occur.

Myeloid sarcoma associated with acute my.normalized_text: Myeloid sarcoma associated with acute myeloid leukemia
Myeloid sarcoma associated with acute my.description: A tumor mass of immature myeloid blasts occurring outside the bone marrow, which can involve skin, lymph nodes, bone, soft tissues, kidneys, and other organs; it may precede detectable acute myeloid leukemia in blood.

Breast cellulitis (nonpurulent mastitis).description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous breast tissue causing diffuse inflammation; ultrasound commonly shows skin thickening and subcutaneous edema without a drainable collection.

Inflammatory breast cancer.description: An aggressive form of breast cancer in which tumor emboli obstruct dermal lymphatics, producing rapid breast redness, edema, enlargement, and peau d'orange-like skin changes.

Breast abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within breast tissue, usually developing as a complication of mastitis or cellulitis and often causing focal pain, fluctuance, and fever.

Breast hematoma or traumatic breast cont.normalized_text: Breast hematoma or traumatic breast contusion
Breast hematoma or traumatic breast cont.description: Bleeding into breast soft tissues after trauma, surgery, anticoagulant use, or a procedure; it may cause swelling, bruising, and tenderness.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome)
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: A severe delayed drug-hypersensitivity reaction characterized by a widespread rash, prominent facial edema, fever, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and possible internal-organ involvement such as hepatitis or nephritis.

Morbilliform drug eruption.description: A common medication-related exanthem causing a symmetric, widespread red maculopapular rash, usually beginning on the trunk and spreading to the limbs; facial involvement may occur.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: An acute medication-triggered skin reaction with widespread erythema and many small sterile pustules, often accompanied by fever and neutrophilia; edema of the face may occur.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A delayed immune-mediated reaction, often caused by medications, that can produce rash, swelling of the hands or face, fever, and joint pain.

Multiple keratoacanthomas (eruptive kera.description: Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing skin tumors that may regress spontaneously but can resemble well-differentiated cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Eruptive forms cause numerous recurrent lesions.

Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.normalized_text: Multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma of Ferguson-Smith
Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.description: A rare inherited or sporadic eruptive keratoacanthoma disorder characterized by repeated crops of locally destructive keratoacanthoma-like tumors that eventually involute, often leaving scars.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthomas of.description: A rare eruptive keratoacanthoma syndrome with many small keratinizing papules that continuously arise over time, often on sun-exposed skin and potentially involving the face and mucous membranes.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.normalized_text: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma-type, multifocal
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant keratinocyte tumor that can present as rapidly enlarging hyperkeratotic nodules or ulcers. Keratoacanthoma-type lesions may be difficult to distinguish histologically and clinically from benign keratoacanthomas.

Syringomyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, often extending over multiple spinal levels and appearing bright on T2-weighted MRI.

Hydromyelia (persistent dilatation of th.normalized_text: Hydromyelia (persistent dilatation of the central canal)
Hydromyelia (persistent dilatation of th.description: Dilatation of the spinal cord's normal central canal containing cerebrospinal fluid; it may be asymptomatic and can resemble a small syrinx on MRI.

Chiari I malformation-associated syringo.description: Syringomyelia caused by impaired cerebrospinal-fluid circulation at the craniovertebral junction, commonly associated with downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL.description: An acute precursor B-cell neoplasm characterized by marrow and peripheral-blood replacement by lymphoblasts. The images show blast-rich marrow and a complex X;14 rearrangement involving Xq22.3, where IRS4 is located, and chromosome 14, consistent with an IGH-associated IRS4 rearrangement.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive neoplasm of immature T-cell precursors that commonly presents with marrow and blood blasts and may have chromosomal rearrangements involving chromosome 14, particularly the T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus at 14q11.2.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), minimally.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), minimally differentiated or undifferentiated subtype
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), minimally.description: AML is a clonal myeloid stem/progenitor-cell malignancy with marrow replacement by blasts and possible circulating blasts. Poorly differentiated AML can morphologically resemble lymphoblastic leukemia until immunophenotyping and molecular studies are performed.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, resulting in cytokine excess, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, and markedly elevated ferritin.

COVID-19-associated hemophagocytic lymph.description: Secondary HLH triggered by severe SARS-CoV-2 infection. Severe COVID-19 can produce diffuse viral pneumonia and, in rare cases, an extreme cytokine-driven hyperinflammatory syndrome with hemophagocytosis.

Epstein-Barr virus-associated hemophagoc.description: A common infectious cause of secondary HLH, particularly associated with acute or reactivated Epstein-Barr virus infection. It causes profound immune activation, cytopenias, liver/spleen enlargement, coagulopathy, and very high ferritin.

Lymphoma-associated hemophagocytic lymph.description: Secondary HLH triggered by an underlying lymphoma, especially T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma. It often presents with severe cytopenias, organomegaly, very high ferritin, coagulopathy, and hemophagocytosis in marrow.

Isolated cortical vein thrombosis with v.normalized_text: Isolated cortical vein thrombosis with venous infarction
Isolated cortical vein thrombosis with v.description: Thrombosis of a superficial cortical cerebral vein can obstruct venous drainage, causing focal cortical edema, hemorrhagic or nonhemorrhagic venous infarction, and abnormal signal within the thrombosed vein.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with cortical venous extension
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.description: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is clot formation in the dural venous sinuses, sometimes extending into cortical veins. It can produce venous congestion, cortical edema, venous infarction, seizures, headache, and intracranial hypertension.

Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.normalized_text: Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortical venous reflux
Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.description: A dural arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal connection between meningeal arteries and dural venous channels. Retrograde cortical venous drainage can cause dilated cortical veins, venous hypertension, edema, and venous infarction.

Acute cortical arterial ischemic infarct.description: An arterial ischemic stroke occurs when an intracranial artery is occluded, producing restricted diffusion and infarction in the affected arterial territory.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, usually causing palpable purpura predominantly on the lower legs and potentially involving the joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.description: A small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, often triggered by medications, infections, autoimmune disease, or malignancy, producing palpable purpura due to neutrophilic injury of superficial dermal vessels.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, and skin; skin lesions may include palpable purpura, ulcers, nodules, or livedo.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, often associated with hepatitis C infection, autoimmune disease, or lymphoproliferative disorders, that commonly causes dependent palpable purpura and may involve nerves, kidneys, and joints.

Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma wi.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma wi.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising in the tonsil or base of tongue/oropharynx, commonly spreading to upper cervical lymph nodes; many cases are associated with human papillomavirus.

HPV-associated tonsillar carcinoma.description: A subtype of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma arising from the palatine or lingual tonsil, often presenting with a neck mass from early lymph-node metastasis.

Cervical lymph node metastasis from an o.normalized_text: Cervical lymph node metastasis from an occult head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
Cervical lymph node metastasis from an o.description: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a cervical lymph node when the primary tumor is small, clinically unapparent, or located in the oropharynx.

Head and neck lymphoma involving cervica.normalized_text: Head and neck lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes and Waldeyer ring
Head and neck lymphoma involving cervica.description: Lymphoma can involve cervical lymph nodes and lymphoid tissue of the tonsils or tongue base, producing FDG-avid soft-tissue masses.

ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymph.normalized_text: ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma involving the urinary bladder
ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymph.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma composed of large pleomorphic 'hallmark' cells, frequently associated with ALK gene rearrangement. It can rarely present as an extranodal bladder mass.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that may rarely arise in or involve the bladder, usually forming a submucosal mass composed of large atypical lymphoid cells.

Primary urothelial carcinoma of the blad.normalized_text: Primary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, poorly differentiated
Primary urothelial carcinoma of the blad.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from urothelial lining cells. Poorly differentiated tumors can form solid sheets of atypical cells and may invade deeply into the bladder wall.

Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma.description: A rare aggressive variant of urothelial carcinoma characterized by discohesive plasmacytoid cells, often infiltrating the bladder wall beneath an apparently intact mucosa.

Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor of the urinary bladder
Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal.description: A rare small round-cell sarcoma that can occur in the bladder and is usually driven by an EWSR1-ETS family gene fusion.

Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.normalized_text: Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip with secondary osteoarthritis
Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.description: Abnormal development of the acetabulum and femoral head/neck can lead to shallow hip sockets, chronic subluxation, deformity, and early degenerative arthritis.

Bilateral Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, ch.description: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head that may heal with flattened, enlarged, and irregular femoral heads and result in early osteoarthritis.

Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosi.normalized_text: Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosis with collapse
Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosi.description: Avascular necrosis occurs when blood supply to the femoral head is impaired, causing bone death, subchondral collapse, femoral-head flattening, and secondary osteoarthritis.

Bilateral primary or secondary hip osteo.normalized_text: Bilateral primary or secondary hip osteoarthritis
Bilateral primary or secondary hip osteo.description: Osteoarthritis is progressive degeneration of articular cartilage with joint-space narrowing, bony remodeling, deformity, and osteophyte formation; in this setting it may be secondary to dysplasia or prior femoral-head disease.

Bipartite patella.description: A congenital/developmental failure of fusion of a secondary patellar ossification center, producing a smooth, well-corticated accessory bone fragment, most often at the superolateral patella.

Patellar fracture.description: An acute break in the patella, usually caused by direct trauma or forceful quadriceps contraction; it may produce pain, swelling, and impaired knee extension.

Symptomatic bipartite patella.description: A bipartite patella that becomes painful after repetitive stress or direct trauma due to inflammation or motion at the fibrocartilaginous junction between the accessory fragment and main patella.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor, most often occurring in young women, with mixed solid and cystic components and characteristic nuclear beta-catenin pathway activation.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A pancreatic neoplasm derived from neuroendocrine cells that may be functioning or nonfunctioning and typically appears as a hypervascular, well-circumscribed solid mass.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: An uncommon malignant epithelial tumor of pancreatic acinar differentiation, usually presenting as a large solid pancreatic mass and confirmed by expression of digestive enzyme markers such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, or BCL10.

Pancreatoblastoma.description: A rare malignant pancreatic tumor with acinar differentiation, primarily occurring in children but occasionally in adults; histology may include acinar structures and characteristic squamoid corpuscles.

Intramuscular venous malformation (intra.normalized_text: Intramuscular venous malformation (intramuscular hemangioma with phleboliths)
Intramuscular venous malformation (intra.description: A low-flow congenital vascular malformation involving muscle or subcutaneous tissue. It can enlarge over time and commonly contains calcified venous thrombi called phleboliths.

Arteriovenous malformation.description: An abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins that may produce a vascular soft-tissue mass, enlarged feeding vessels, skin discoloration, and increased flow on vascular imaging.

Soft-tissue venous hemangioma.description: A benign vascular lesion, often now classified within the venous-malformation spectrum, that can occur in skeletal muscle and present as a bluish compressible mass with phleboliths.

Tumoral calcinosis.description: A disorder characterized by periarticular deposition of calcium phosphate in lobulated soft tissues, often around large joints such as the hip.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma or other calc.normalized_text: Extraskeletal osteosarcoma or other calcified soft-tissue sarcoma
Extraskeletal osteosarcoma or other calc.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue tumor that can form mineralized or ossified material and present as an enlarging deep soft-tissue mass.

Knee osteoarthritis.description: Degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, joint-space narrowing, marginal osteophytes, and subchondral bone remodeling.

Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the kne.description: Degenerative arthritis developing after prior knee injury, such as ligamentous injury, meniscal injury, or an intra-articular fracture; radiographs can resemble primary osteoarthritis.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.description: Crystal deposition disease that can produce chronic degenerative arthropathy of the knee, sometimes with an osteoarthritis-like radiographic appearance and chondrocalcinosis.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor, most commonly arising in the uterus, composed of intersecting bundles of spindle-shaped smooth-muscle cells and typically positive for smooth-muscle immunostains such as SMA and desmin.

Leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor characterized by spindle-cell fascicles with cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and/or tumor necrosis; it commonly expresses smooth-muscle markers including SMA and desmin.

Smooth Muscle Tumor of Uncertain Maligna.normalized_text: Smooth Muscle Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential (STUMP)
Smooth Muscle Tumor of Uncertain Maligna.description: A uterine smooth-muscle neoplasm with histologic features that do not meet definitive criteria for either benign leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma, often showing atypia or other concerning features without unequivocal malignancy.

SHORT syndrome.description: A rare PIK3R1-related disorder characterized by short stature, partial lipodystrophy, distinctive progeroid facial features, delayed dentition, and sometimes insulin resistance. SHORT refers to Short stature, Hyperextensibility/hernia, Ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and Teething delay.

Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome.description: A neonatal progeroid syndrome causing prenatal or early postnatal growth failure, generalized loss of subcutaneous fat, aged-appearing wrinkled skin, sparse hair, and characteristic craniofacial and dental abnormalities.

Russell-Silver syndrome.description: A genetic growth disorder characterized by fetal and postnatal growth restriction, relative macrocephaly or prominent forehead, triangular face, feeding difficulty, body asymmetry in some patients, and delayed bone maturation.

Mandibuloacral dysplasia with lipodystro.description: A laminopathy-associated progeroid disorder involving growth retardation, craniofacial abnormalities, mandibular hypoplasia, mottled or thin skin, partial lipodystrophy, and skeletal abnormalities including delayed bone maturation or acro-osteolysis.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agam.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by impaired B-cell maturation, most often due to BTK gene mutations. It results in profoundly reduced or absent circulating B cells and very low immunoglobulins, causing recurrent bacterial respiratory infections and bronchiectasis.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: An acquired adult-onset immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, absent or markedly reduced B cells, and variable T-cell abnormalities, especially reduced CD4 cells.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A heterogeneous primary antibody deficiency characterized by low immunoglobulin levels, impaired antibody responses, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and frequent development of bronchiectasis. B-cell numbers may be low but are usually not completely absent.

Secondary B-cell depletion due to anti-C.normalized_text: Secondary B-cell depletion due to anti-CD20 therapy or another acquired cause of hypogammaglobulinemia
Secondary B-cell depletion due to anti-C.description: Anti-CD20 medications such as rituximab can markedly deplete circulating CD19-positive B cells and may cause prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia, recurrent respiratory infections, and bronchiectasis in susceptible patients.

Type B1 thymoma (lymphocyte-rich thymoma.description: A thymic epithelial tumor of the anterior mediastinum characterized by abundant immature T lymphocytes with scattered neoplastic epithelial cells.

Micronodular thymoma with lymphoid strom.description: An uncommon thymoma composed of small epithelial tumor nodules embedded in prominent lymphoid stroma, often containing abundant lymphocytes and sometimes germinal centers.

Thymic hyperplasia.description: Benign enlargement of thymic tissue that may show preserved thymic architecture with epithelial cells, immature T lymphocytes, and Hassall corpuscles.

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma involving the m.description: An aggressive malignancy of immature T-cell precursors that commonly presents as an anterior mediastinal mass and can resemble thymic tumors histologically.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the thymus, usually presenting as an anterior mediastinal mass and showing overtly atypical epithelial cells with relatively fewer immature lymphocytes than thymoma.

Massive acute pulmonary embolism with ac.normalized_text: Massive acute pulmonary embolism with acute right-heart strain
Massive acute pulmonary embolism with ac.description: Obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation by thrombus, causing acute right-ventricular failure, hypoxemia, shock, cardiac arrest, and myocardial injury from severe right-heart strain.

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiog.normalized_text: Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock
Acute myocardial infarction with cardiog.description: Acute myocardial necrosis caused by coronary artery occlusion or severe coronary ischemia, potentially resulting in malignant arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, pulmonary edema, and shock.

Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo.description: A transient acute left-ventricular systolic dysfunction triggered by severe physical or emotional stress, often mimicking acute myocardial infarction despite nonobstructive coronary arteries.

Post-cardiac-arrest syndrome with ischem.normalized_text: Post-cardiac-arrest syndrome with ischemia-reperfusion injury and rhabdomyolysis
Post-cardiac-arrest syndrome with ischem.description: Multiorgan injury after successful resuscitation from cardiac arrest, caused by global hypoperfusion, ischemia-reperfusion injury, muscle injury from prolonged arrest or CPR, and systemic inflammatory activation.

Acute superior mesenteric vein thrombosi.normalized_text: Acute superior mesenteric vein thrombosis with mesenteric venous ischemia
Acute superior mesenteric vein thrombosi.description: Thrombotic occlusion of the superior mesenteric venous system can impair intestinal venous drainage, causing bowel-wall edema, ischemia, and potentially infarction. Doppler and CT findings may show absent or disturbed venous flow and intraluminal thrombus.

Portal vein thrombosis.description: Portal vein thrombosis is obstruction of portal venous blood flow by thrombus. It may be acute or chronic and can extend into the splenic or superior mesenteric veins. It can lead to portal hypertension, intestinal congestion, and hepatic encephalopathy in patients with underlying liver disease.

Acute mesenteric ischemia due to mesente.normalized_text: Acute mesenteric ischemia due to mesenteric venous obstruction
Acute mesenteric ischemia due to mesente.description: Mesenteric ischemia occurs when intestinal blood supply or venous drainage is compromised. In mesenteric venous thrombosis, venous congestion may cause bowel-wall edema, hemorrhage, ischemia, pneumatosis, and eventual bowel infarction.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive skin eruption characterized by slowly expanding annular red plaques, often with central clearing and a fine trailing scale on the inner edge.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection that causes circular, scaly plaques with an active raised border and central clearing.

Urticaria multiforme.description: A benign hypersensitivity reaction seen mainly in infants and young children, producing transient annular or polycyclic erythematous wheals, sometimes with dusky centers.

Erythema multiforme.description: An immune-mediated eruption, often following infection, characterized by target-like lesions with concentric zones of color; it commonly affects the extremities but can involve the trunk.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wil.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually caused by a reduced aortomesenteric angle and distance, producing proximal intestinal obstruction.

Mechanical duodenal obstruction.description: A blockage of the duodenum that causes upstream dilation of the stomach and proximal duodenum; causes include extrinsic vascular compression, mass lesions, inflammatory strictures, or congenital bands.

Gastric outlet obstruction.description: Obstruction at the pylorus or proximal duodenum causing retention of gastric contents and gastric dilatation. Common causes include peptic ulcer-related scarring, malignancy, or severe inflammation.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying due to impaired gastric motility, often associated with diabetes, medications, neurologic disease, or prior gastric surgery.

Gastrocolic fistula.description: An abnormal communication between the stomach (or gastric pouch) and colon, allowing gastric contents or contrast material to pass directly into the colon. It may occur from peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, inflammatory disease, or postoperative complications.

Postoperative gastrocolic fistula after.normalized_text: Postoperative gastrocolic fistula after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Postoperative gastrocolic fistula after.description: A rare late complication of gastric bypass surgery in which a fistula develops between the gastric pouch or gastrojejunal anastomotic region and the transverse colon, often related to marginal ulceration or chronic inflammation.

Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the.normalized_text: Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the colon
Marginal ulcer with fistulization to the.description: A marginal ulcer is ulceration near a gastrojejunal anastomosis after gastric bypass surgery. Severe chronic ulceration can erode into adjacent structures, including the transverse colon, producing a gastrocolic fistula.

Gastric malignancy with gastrocolic fist.description: Advanced gastric cancer can invade through the gastric wall into the adjacent transverse colon, creating a gastrocolic fistula. This is an important alternative cause of a gastric-to-colonic fistula, particularly in patients without prior surgery.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), including emphysema
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: A chronic lung disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, often associated with smoking. Chest radiographs may show hyperinflation and chronically increased bronchovascular markings.

Chronic bronchitis.description: A COPD phenotype involving chronic airway inflammation and mucus production, typically causing chronic productive cough and increased peribronchial markings on imaging.

Normal chest radiograph.description: A chest radiograph without acute cardiopulmonary abnormality; mild chronic bronchovascular prominence can be nonspecific or related to technique.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive photosensitive skin eruptions and, in many patients, proximal muscle weakness. Cutaneous disease may occur without clinically apparent muscle disease.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus.description: A photosensitive autoimmune skin disorder causing widespread annular or papulosquamous erythematous lesions, most often on sun-exposed areas of the neck, chest, shoulders, and arms.

Photocontact dermatitis or chronic actin.normalized_text: Photocontact dermatitis or chronic actinic dermatitis
Photocontact dermatitis or chronic actin.description: An eczematous inflammatory reaction triggered or worsened by ultraviolet light, sometimes related to topical products, fragrances, medications, or sunscreen exposure.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutane.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutaneous manifestations
Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutane.description: A systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease that can cause photosensitive rashes, inflammatory arthritis, oral ulcers, kidney disease, blood-count abnormalities, and other organ involvement.

Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X.normalized_text: Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X (Agammaglobulinemia de Bruton)
Agammaglobulinemia ligada al cromosoma X.description: Una inmunodeficiencia primaria causada por variantes patógenas en el gen BTK ligado al cromosoma X, que conduce a una maduración deteriorada de las células B y a una producción notablemente reducida de todas las clases de inmunoglobulinas.

Agammaglobulinemia autosómica recesiva.description: Un grupo de trastornos hereditarios causados por defectos en los genes necesarios para el desarrollo temprano de células B, como IGHM, CD79A, CD79B, BLNK, PIK3R1 o genes relacionados, que resultan en una grave deficiencia de anticuerpos y baja o ausente presencia de células B maduras.

Inmunodeficiencia variable común (CVID).description: Un trastorno heterogéneo de deficiencia de anticuerpos caracterizado por un bajo IgG con bajos IgA y/o IgM, respuestas específicas de anticuerpos deterioradas y anomalías variables en las células B; normalmente se presenta más tarde en la infancia o la edad adulta.

Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.normalized_text: Penile fracture (rupture of the right corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea)
Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.description: Traumatic tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually causing blood to escape into surrounding penile and scrotal soft tissues.

Traumatic penile and scrotal soft-tissue.normalized_text: Traumatic penile and scrotal soft-tissue hematoma without complete corporal rupture
Traumatic penile and scrotal soft-tissue.description: Bleeding into penile or scrotal soft tissues after trauma, which can produce swelling and bruising but does not necessarily involve disruption of the tunica albuginea.

Isolated dorsal penile vein injury.description: Traumatic rupture of a superficial or deep dorsal penile vein can cause penile bruising and hematoma and may clinically resemble penile fracture, but the corpora cavernosa and tunica albuginea are generally intact.

Hidrocefalia obstructiva debido a esteno.normalized_text: Hidrocefalia obstructiva debido a estenosis acueductal
Hidrocefalia obstructiva debido a esteno.description: La obstrucción o estrechamiento del acueducto cerebral provoca un flujo cefalorraquídeo alterado del tercer al cuarto ventrículo, provocando agrandamiento de los ventrículos lateral y tercer.

Neurocisticercosis intraventricular con.description: La neurocisticercosis es una infección del sistema nervioso central por larvas de Taenia solium. Un quiste dentro del sistema ventricular puede obstruir el foramen de Monro, el tercer ventrículo o el acueducto cerebral y causar hidrocefalia.

Quiste del tercer ventrículo o acueducto.normalized_text: Quiste del tercer ventrículo o acueducto que causa hidrocefalia obstructiva
Quiste del tercer ventrículo o acueducto.description: Una lesión quística benigna, como un quiste aracnoide, ependímico o neuroepitelial, puede obstruir las vías del líquido cefalorraquídeo en el tercer ventrículo o acueducto y producir ventriculomegalia aguas arriba.

Glioma de placas tectales que causa obst.normalized_text: Glioma de placas tectales que causa obstrucción acueductal
Glioma de placas tectales que causa obst.description: Un glioma de bajo grado que afecta a la región tectal puede comprimir u obstruir el acueducto cerebral, causando generalmente una hidrocefalia obstructiva progresiva lenta.

Endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endom.description: A malignant gland-forming tumor arising from the endometrial lining of the uterus. It may form a pelvic/uterine mass and can spread to the peritoneal cavity in advanced disease.

High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary.normalized_text: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneum
High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary.description: An aggressive Müllerian adenocarcinoma that commonly presents as a pelvic mass with peritoneal spread, ascites, and malignant cells in fluid cytology.

Cervical adenocarcinoma.description: A glandular cancer arising from the cervix, often associated with high-risk human papillomavirus. Advanced tumors can extend into the uterus, parametrial tissues, pelvic nodes, or peritoneal cavity.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma involving the pelvis or peritoneum
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma inv.description: A colorectal gland-forming malignancy may metastasize to the pelvis, ovaries, peritoneum, or ascitic fluid and can produce malignant glandular cells on cytology.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolality gap, and accumulation of glycolate and oxalate metabolites. Some lactate assays may falsely report very high lactate due to glycolate interference.

Methanol poisoning.description: Methanol ingestion produces formic acid accumulation, causing severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and an elevated osmolality gap. Visual symptoms and neurologic impairment may occur but are not provided.

Propylene glycol poisoning.description: Propylene glycol toxicity, often from intravenous medication solvents or ingestion, can cause hyperosmolality, an increased osmolality gap, lactic acidosis, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Diethylene glycol poisoning.description: Diethylene glycol is a toxic alcohol that initially causes an elevated osmolality gap and metabolic acidosis; delayed toxicity commonly includes acute kidney injury and neurologic complications.

Alcoholic ketoacidosis.description: Alcoholic ketoacidosis occurs after heavy alcohol use with poor nutritional intake and vomiting, producing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and often elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate. The osmolality gap may be increased from ethanol or other alcohols.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Uterine leiomyosarcoma.description: An aggressive malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the uterus that can form a large heterogeneous pelvic mass with necrosis and hemorrhage. It may cause systemic inflammatory findings and anemia.

Undifferentiated uterine sarcoma.description: A rare high-grade uterine mesenchymal malignancy composed of poorly differentiated malignant cells. These tumors often present as large rapidly growing masses with extensive necrosis and can produce inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.description: A mesenchymal tumor composed of myofibroblastic spindle-to-epithelioid cells with a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. It can occur in the pelvis or female genital tract and may cause fever, anemia, leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Ovarian carcinoma or primary ovarian sar.normalized_text: Ovarian carcinoma or primary ovarian sarcoma with paraneoplastic inflammatory response
Ovarian carcinoma or primary ovarian sar.description: A malignant ovarian tumor can present as a large complex pelvic mass with necrosis, hemorrhage, anemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Some tumors produce cytokines such as G-CSF, causing neutrophilic leukocytosis.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, leading to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and progressive coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and organ involvement.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syn.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, resulting in dermatan and heparan sulfate accumulation and progressive multisystem disease.

Mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease).description: A severe autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking disorder caused by deficient N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, resulting in accumulation of multiple lysosomal substrates in cells.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (Maroteaux.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by arylsulfatase B deficiency, producing dermatan sulfate accumulation with coarse facies, skeletal disease, and organ involvement.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A fibroinflammatory disorder causing plaque-like soft-tissue thickening around the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels, often encasing and obstructing the ureters.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: An immune-mediated form of retroperitoneal fibrosis associated with IgG4-related disease; it can produce inflammatory soft tissue surrounding the aorta, iliac arteries, and ureters.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can produce confluent retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or infiltrative soft tissue that surrounds vessels and may compress or obstruct the ureters.

Metastatic retroperitoneal lymphadenopat.description: Metastatic cancer involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes can form soft-tissue masses that compress the ureters or adjacent vessels.

Right-sided lobar pneumonia.description: Acute infection of lung parenchyma causing alveolar consolidation, commonly with air bronchograms and unilateral opacity on chest radiography.

Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an end.normalized_text: Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an endobronchial obstruction
Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an end.description: Pneumonia developing distal to obstruction of a bronchus, which may be caused by mucus plugging, an aspirated foreign body, or an endobronchial tumor.

Right lung atelectasis.description: Collapse or incomplete expansion of lung tissue, often caused by bronchial obstruction, compression, or postoperative hypoventilation; it may produce unilateral opacity and mediastinal shift toward the affected side.

Aspiration pneumonia.description: Pulmonary infection or inflammation caused by inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents, often affecting dependent portions of the right lung.

Fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease causing alternating areas of stenosis and dilation, classically producing a 'string-of-beads' appearance in renal, carotid, vertebral, and other medium-sized arteries.

Segmental arterial mediolysis.description: A rare noninflammatory arteriopathy of medium-to-large abdominal arteries characterized by arterial dissections, aneurysms, stenoses, and irregular beading, often involving splanchnic vessels.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis affecting medium-sized muscular arteries that can cause multiple microaneurysms, stenoses, thrombosis, and ischemia, particularly in renal and mesenteric vessels.

Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachyc.description: A rapid ventricular-origin rhythm with regular, broad QRS complexes of similar morphology; this is the most concerning and likely interpretation of a regular wide-complex tachycardia.

Supraventricular tachycardia with bundle.normalized_text: Supraventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block aberrancy
Supraventricular tachycardia with bundle.description: A supraventricular rhythm such as AV nodal reentrant tachycardia or atrial tachycardia that conducts through an abnormal intraventricular pathway, producing a wide-QRS tachycardia.

Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant ta.normalized_text: Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia due to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant ta.description: A reentrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway for antegrade conduction, causing a regular broad-complex tachycardia that can mimic ventricular tachycardia.

Ventricular flutter.description: An extremely rapid ventricular tachyarrhythmia, usually with very broad repetitive waveforms and little separation between QRS complexes; it may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation.

Fetal ventriculomegaly.description: Abnormal enlargement of the fetal lateral cerebral ventricles, usually defined by an atrial ventricular width of 10 mm or greater on prenatal ultrasound.

Fetal hydrocephalus.description: Progressive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system, causing ventricular enlargement and potentially increased intracranial pressure.

Agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus cal.normalized_text: Agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum with colpocephaly
Agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus cal.description: Partial or complete absence or abnormal development of the corpus callosum, often associated with disproportionate enlargement of the posterior horns of the lateral ventricles (colpocephaly).

Aqueductal stenosis.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct that impairs cerebrospinal fluid flow and commonly causes enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce granulomatous inflammation, often with upper-lobe disease and sometimes hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that may cause pulmonary granulomas and hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, particularly after environmental exposure.

Lunotriquetral ligament tear.description: Injury or degeneration of the ligament connecting the lunate and triquetrum, which can cause carpal instability and ulnar-sided wrist pain. The arrow appears to indicate the lunotriquetral interval/ligament.

Lunotriquetral instability.description: Abnormal motion between the lunate and triquetrum, usually resulting from lunotriquetral ligament injury; it may produce chronic ulnar-sided wrist pain, clicking, or weakness.

Degenerative lunotriquetral ligament inj.description: Chronic wear or partial degeneration of the lunotriquetral ligament, sometimes associated with repetitive wrist loading or age-related intercarpal degeneration.

Bilateral internal watershed (border-zon.description: Ischemic strokes affecting the deep white matter between major cerebral arterial territories, usually caused by reduced cerebral perfusion rather than embolic occlusion of one artery.

Moyamoya disease or moyamoya syndrome wi.normalized_text: Moyamoya disease or moyamoya syndrome with hypoperfusion-related infarction
Moyamoya disease or moyamoya syndrome wi.description: A progressive narrowing of the terminal internal carotid arteries and proximal cerebral arteries that causes impaired cerebral blood flow, collateral vessel formation, and recurrent watershed ischemic strokes.

Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury due to sys.normalized_text: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury due to systemic hypotension or hypoxemia
Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury due to sys.description: Global reduction in oxygen delivery or cerebral perfusion can selectively injure watershed regions, particularly the deep white matter, producing bilateral symmetric diffusion restriction.

Hepatic angiomyolipoma (epithelioid angi.description: A rare benign mesenchymal liver tumor composed variably of blood vessels, smooth-muscle-like epithelioid cells, and fat. Some lesions contain little or no visible fat and can mimic hepatocellular carcinoma on contrast imaging.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes, most often occurring in patients with chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or other chronic liver disease. It commonly appears as an arterial-phase enhancing liver mass with later washout.

Hepatic adenoma.description: A benign hepatocellular neoplasm that may occur in women and can be associated with estrogen exposure, anabolic steroids, obesity, or metabolic disorders. It may appear as a well-defined hypervascular liver mass and can occasionally bleed.

Focal nodular hyperplasia.description: A benign hyperplastic hepatic lesion thought to result from a localized vascular abnormality. It is commonly incidentally detected and often shows strong arterial enhancement, sometimes with a central scar.

Linear morphea (linear scleroderma of th.normalized_text: Linear morphea (linear scleroderma of the scalp)
Linear morphea (linear scleroderma of th.description: A localized sclerosing connective-tissue disorder that can form linear bands of inflamed, indurated skin with scarring hair loss when it affects the scalp.

Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.normalized_text: Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus profundus) with scarring alopecia
Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.description: A chronic form of cutaneous lupus involving deep dermis and subcutaneous fat, which may cause inflammatory plaques, fat inflammation, atrophy, and permanent scarring alopecia on the scalp.

Lichen planopilaris (linear or blaschkoi.description: A lymphocyte-mediated cicatricial alopecia in which inflammation targets hair follicles, producing perifollicular redness and progressive permanent hair loss; rarely it may follow a linear distribution.

Alopecia areata.description: An autoimmune, nonscarring hair-loss disorder that usually produces sharply demarcated patches of hair loss and may show a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate on histology.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.normalized_text: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) with gastrointestinal involvement
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: A small-vessel immune-mediated vasculitis that commonly affects children and may cause bowel-wall edema, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, intussusception, and renal involvement.

Small-bowel intussusception.description: Invagination of one segment of bowel into another, which can produce bowel obstruction, bowel-wall edema, and a characteristic target or concentric-ring appearance on CT.

Enteritis with small-bowel ileus.description: Inflammatory or infectious inflammation of the small intestine can cause bowel-wall thickening, edema, fluid-filled bowel loops, and functional ileus.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.normalized_text: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the left anterior descending coronary artery
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary-artery wall that narrows the true lumen and can cause acute coronary syndrome. SCAD is strongly associated with fibromuscular dysplasia.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) secondary to SCAD
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction without persistent ST-segment elevation, caused here by impaired coronary blood flow from spontaneous coronary artery dissection rather than plaque rupture.

Renal-artery fibromuscular dysplasia (FM.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease causing alternating areas of stenosis and dilation, often producing a 'string-of-beads' appearance in renal arteries and associated with SCAD.

Vesicoureteral reflux.description: Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into one or both ureters and potentially the renal collecting systems, commonly demonstrated during a voiding cystourethrogram.

Posterior urethral valves.description: A congenital obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra of male infants and children that causes bladder outlet obstruction, bladder trabeculation, hydroureteronephrosis, and often vesicoureteral reflux.

Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesico.normalized_text: Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesicoureteral reflux
Neurogenic bladder with secondary vesico.description: Bladder dysfunction due to impaired neurologic control can produce high intravesical pressure, incomplete emptying, bladder wall irregularity, and reflux into the ureters and kidneys.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle inflammation and distinctive cutaneous findings; severe cases can cause marked subcutaneous and muscular edema.

Edematous dermatomyositis.description: A rare, severe presentation of dermatomyositis in which generalized or regional subcutaneous edema accompanies inflammatory myopathy and typical dermatomyositis skin findings.

Angioedema.description: Acute swelling of deep dermal and submucosal tissues, commonly affecting the eyelids, lips, tongue, face, and upper airway; it may be allergic, medication-related, or bradykinin-mediated.

Infectious myositis or deep neck space i.normalized_text: Infectious myositis or deep neck space infection
Infectious myositis or deep neck space i.description: Bacterial infection involving muscles or deep cervical tissues can produce painful swelling, inflammatory edema, lymph-node enlargement, and potential airway compromise.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis overlap
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can occasionally overlap with inflammatory myopathy and cause facial rash, edema, vasculitic lesions, and muscle inflammation.

Nonbullous impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, characterized by fragile blisters or erosions that develop classic honey-colored crusts.

Bullous impetigo.description: A toxin-mediated staphylococcal skin infection that produces fragile fluid-filled blisters which rupture, leaving moist erosions and yellow-brown crusting.

Allergic contact dermatitis with seconda.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis with secondary impetiginization
Allergic contact dermatitis with seconda.description: An inflammatory skin reaction caused by contact with an allergen, such as adhesive material, plants, topical products, or metals; scratching and skin breakdown can lead to secondary bacterial infection and crusting.

Ecthyma.description: A deeper ulcerative form of impetigo in which bacterial infection extends into the dermis, producing crusted sores that may heal with scarring.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by long-term deposition of monosodium urate crystals, producing large firm tophi around joints, fingers, tendons, and soft tissues.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that commonly affects small joints of the hands symmetrically and can cause deformity; firm rheumatoid nodules may occur in some patients.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare systemic histiocytic disorder that can cause destructive symmetric polyarthritis and papulonodular skin lesions around the hands and fingers.

Calcinosis cutis associated with systemi.normalized_text: Calcinosis cutis associated with systemic sclerosis or dermatomyositis
Calcinosis cutis associated with systemi.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and soft tissue, sometimes associated with connective-tissue diseases, which can form hard periarticular nodules and impair hand function.

Thymoma.description: A tumor arising from thymic epithelial cells, typically presenting as a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass in adults. It may be associated with myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune disorders.

Mediastinal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma involving mediastinal lymph nodes or thymic tissue, often causing an anterior mediastinal mass. Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma are important considerations.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A rare aggressive malignant epithelial tumor of the thymus that can appear as an irregular anterior mediastinal mass and may invade nearby structures.

Mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A tumor derived from germ cells that can occur in the anterior mediastinum. Teratomas may contain fat or calcification, while seminomatous and nonseminomatous tumors are usually soft-tissue masses.

Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thy.normalized_text: Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thyroid tissue
Substernal thyroid goiter or ectopic thy.description: Enlarged thyroid tissue extending into the upper mediastinum, or rarely ectopic thyroid tissue, can produce an anterior mediastinal mass.

Viral bronchiolitis or viral bronchitis.description: A viral lower-airway infection causing inflammation of the bronchioles, often producing peribronchial thickening and bilateral perihilar interstitial markings on chest radiography.

Reactive airway disease / asthma exacerb.description: Inflammatory narrowing of the airways that can cause hyperinflation and prominent peribronchial markings, particularly during an acute exacerbation.

Atypical pneumonia.description: A pneumonia caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae or certain viruses, often producing diffuse or perihilar interstitial infiltrates rather than a dense focal lobar opacity.

Chronic bronchitic airway inflammation.description: Inflammation and thickening of the bronchial walls, which may produce increased perihilar bronchovascular markings on chest radiographs.

Right-sided pulmonary venous obstruction.normalized_text: Right-sided pulmonary venous obstruction/stenosis with unilateral pulmonary edema
Right-sided pulmonary venous obstruction.description: Obstruction or narrowing of a pulmonary vein can cause elevated venous pressure in the affected lung, producing unilateral interstitial edema, septal thickening, and pleural effusion.

Unilateral cardiogenic pulmonary edema,.normalized_text: Unilateral cardiogenic pulmonary edema, potentially related to mitral regurgitation
Unilateral cardiogenic pulmonary edema,.description: Pulmonary edema from elevated left-sided cardiac filling pressures usually affects both lungs, but severe eccentric mitral regurgitation can preferentially direct flow toward the right upper pulmonary veins and cause right-sided edema.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis.description: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis is metastatic tumor spread through pulmonary lymphatic vessels, producing interlobular septal and peribronchovascular thickening, often with an asymmetric or unilateral distribution.

Right diaphragmatic eventration.description: Congenital or acquired abnormal elevation of an intact hemidiaphragm due to thinning or weakness of diaphragmatic muscle, often affecting the right side.

Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilat.normalized_text: Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis
Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilat.description: Loss of phrenic nerve function produces weakness or paralysis of one hemidiaphragm, resulting in persistent unilateral diaphragmatic elevation.

Right lower-lobe atelectasis with second.normalized_text: Right lower-lobe atelectasis with secondary diaphragmatic elevation
Right lower-lobe atelectasis with second.description: Partial collapse or volume loss of the right lower lobe can pull the right hemidiaphragm upward and produce basilar opacity.

Subpulmonic pleural effusion.description: Pleural fluid accumulating beneath the lung base can mimic elevation of a hemidiaphragm on chest radiography.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation, frequently involving the oral cavity and presenting as a rapidly enlarging ulcerated oral or maxillary mass. Tumor cells commonly express MUM1 and may have variable BCL6/CD10 expression.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.description: A common aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can arise extranodally in the oral cavity, jaw, gingiva, palate, or maxillary sinus and can cause destructive bone and soft-tissue masses.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma that may involve the jaws and oral cavity, particularly in endemic or immunodeficiency-associated settings. It typically shows a very high proliferation rate and germinal-center phenotype.

Extramedullary plasmacytoma.description: A localized neoplasm of monoclonal plasma cells that can occur in the upper aerodigestive tract or oral cavity and may produce an oral mass with adjacent bone erosion.

Tinea corporis with tinea cruris (dermat.description: A superficial fungal infection of keratinized skin caused by dermatophytes, producing expanding annular plaques with an active scaly border and central clearing; groin involvement is termed tinea cruris.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly enlarging annular red patches or plaques, often with central clearing and a trailing scale inside the advancing edge.

Annular psoriasis.description: A less common morphologic form of psoriasis in which erythematous plaques develop ring-shaped borders with partial central clearing; lesions usually have scale and may coalesce.

Gastric outlet obstruction due to gastri.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction due to gastric adenocarcinoma (antral/pyloric cancer, possibly diffuse-type)
Gastric outlet obstruction due to gastri.description: Gastric adenocarcinoma involving the distal stomach can narrow the antrum or pylorus, producing gastric outlet obstruction with marked retention and dilatation of the stomach. Diffuse infiltrative cancer can also cause thickened, nodular gastric folds.

Adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: Adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is an uncommon cause of gastric outlet obstruction in which hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle produces narrowing of the pyloric channel and severe gastric retention.

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.normalized_text: Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) causing gastric outlet obstruction
Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A gastric GIST is a mesenchymal tumor arising from the muscularis propria. A tumor near the antrum or pylorus can obstruct gastric emptying and may appear as a submucosal or intramural mass with preserved or distorted overlying mucosa.

Gastric lymphoma.description: Primary gastric lymphoma can produce diffuse or focal gastric wall thickening, enlarged folds, and occasionally obstruction when the distal stomach is involved. It may mimic adenocarcinoma endoscopically and radiographically.

Undetermined genetic variant.description: The image shows Sanger sequencing chromatograms for a child and both parents, suggesting evaluation of a possible nucleotide variant. A specific disease cannot be identified without the gene name, exact variant, zygosity interpretation, and clinical phenotype.

Acute middle cerebral artery ischemic st.normalized_text: Acute middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke
Acute middle cerebral artery ischemic st.description: Acute cerebral infarction caused by occlusion of the middle cerebral artery, producing early ischemic changes in the affected cerebral hemisphere.

Large-vessel intracranial arterial throm.normalized_text: Large-vessel intracranial arterial thrombosis or embolic occlusion
Large-vessel intracranial arterial throm.description: Occlusion of a major intracranial artery by an embolus or in-situ thrombus, commonly causing an acute territorial ischemic infarct.

Acute right hemispheric cerebral infarct.normalized_text: Acute right hemispheric cerebral infarction with early edema
Acute right hemispheric cerebral infarct.description: Acute loss of blood supply to part of the cerebral hemisphere, resulting in cytotoxic edema and reduced distinction between cortical gray matter and white matter on noncontrast CT.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the stomach
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from gastrointestinal pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal), most commonly in the stomach. GISTs typically express KIT (CD117) and DOG1 and may show high proliferative activity in malignant tumors.

Gastric leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can occur in the stomach and form a bulky abdominal mass. It is usually positive for smooth-muscle markers such as SMA and desmin rather than KIT/DOG1.

Gastric lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm involving the stomach, which can present as gastric wall thickening or a mass. Diagnosis is supported by lymphoid morphology and leukocyte-marker expression rather than KIT/DOG1 expression.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A severe hyperinflammatory syndrome in which activated macrophages and T cells cause systemic inflammation and may phagocytose blood cells in the bone marrow or other tissues.

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), of.normalized_text: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), often associated with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease
Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), of.description: MAS is a form of secondary HLH caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, commonly complicating systemic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

Viral-associated secondary hemophagocyti.description: HLH can be triggered by viral infections, particularly Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, influenza, and other systemic viral illnesses; rash may accompany the underlying infection.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with second.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with secondary macrophage activation syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus with second.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease that can cause cutaneous eruptions and, rarely, trigger secondary HLH/MAS with hemophagocytosis.

Paget disease of bone involving the skul.normalized_text: Paget disease of bone involving the skull
Paget disease of bone involving the skul.description: A chronic disorder of excessive and disorganized bone remodeling that can cause skull enlargement, cortical thickening, mixed lytic-sclerotic "cotton wool" changes, cranial nerve compression, and basilar invagination.

Craniofacial fibrous dysplasia.description: A benign developmental bone disorder in which normal bone is replaced by fibro-osseous tissue, producing expansile bone remodeling and a ground-glass appearance; it may involve one or multiple craniofacial bones.

Renal osteodystrophy with secondary hype.description: Skeletal changes caused by chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism, which can produce altered skull mineralization, a salt-and-pepper skull appearance, bone resorption, and diffuse skeletal disease.

Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.normalized_text: Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct blocks cerebrospinal-fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, producing marked enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aque.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aqueductal web or membranous aqueductal obstruction
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aque.description: A thin congenital membrane or web within the cerebral aqueduct can create partial or intermittent obstruction of cerebrospinal-fluid flow, causing triventricular hydrocephalus and potentially episodic worsening.

Intermittently decompensated chronic hyd.description: Chronic hydrocephalus may remain partly compensated for a period and then cause episodic clinical deterioration when cerebrospinal-fluid pressure rises or compensatory mechanisms fail.

Mitochondrial cytopathy with episodic la.normalized_text: Mitochondrial cytopathy with episodic lactic acidosis
Mitochondrial cytopathy with episodic la.description: Mitochondrial disorders impair oxidative energy production and can cause recurrent metabolic decompensation with elevated lactate, anion-gap acidosis, neurologic manifestations, and secondary carnitine depletion.

Organic acidemia, such as propionic acid.normalized_text: Organic acidemia, such as propionic acidemia or methylmalonic acidemia
