Organic acidemia, such as propionic acid.description: Organic acidemias are inherited metabolic disorders that may cause episodic high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and secondary depletion of free carnitine, especially during illness or fasting.

Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome).description: A disorder of excessive aldosterone activity, usually caused by an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, leading to suppressed renin and often hypertension and hypokalemia.

ACTH-independent cortisol secretion from.normalized_text: ACTH-independent cortisol secretion from an adrenal adenoma
ACTH-independent cortisol secretion from.description: An adrenal cortical adenoma can autonomously produce cortisol, suppressing pituitary ACTH. This may cause overt Cushing syndrome or milder autonomous cortisol secretion.

Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (subc.normalized_text: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (subclinical Cushing syndrome)
Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (subc.description: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion is low-grade cortisol production by an adrenal lesion without the full clinical features of overt Cushing syndrome. ACTH may be suppressed and cortisol testing can be variably abnormal.

Mixed aldosterone- and cortisol-secretin.normalized_text: Mixed aldosterone- and cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
Mixed aldosterone- and cortisol-secretin.description: A functional adrenal cortical adenoma may rarely co-secrete aldosterone and cortisol, producing biochemical evidence of primary aldosteronism together with ACTH suppression or increased cortisol production.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing tumor of adrenal medullary cells that can cause episodic hypertension, headaches, palpitations, sweating, and elevated metanephrine levels.

Acute anterior ST-segment elevation myoc.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI), likely proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion
Acute anterior ST-segment elevation myoc.description: An acute heart attack caused by abrupt coronary artery blockage, producing transmural ischemia of the anterior wall of the left ventricle.

Acute anteroseptal myocardial infarction.description: A subtype of acute anterior myocardial infarction involving the interventricular septum, usually due to occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery.

Hyperkalemia.description: Elevated serum potassium that can cause characteristic ECG changes including tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, and eventually sine-wave morphology.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the pericardium that commonly causes diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression.

Sigmoid volvulus with large-bowel obstru.normalized_text: Sigmoid volvulus with large-bowel obstruction, complicated by perforation
Sigmoid volvulus with large-bowel obstru.description: Twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery causes a closed-loop large-bowel obstruction. Progressive distention can lead to ischemia, necrosis, and bowel perforation.

Cecal volvulus with bowel obstruction an.normalized_text: Cecal volvulus with bowel obstruction and possible perforation
Cecal volvulus with bowel obstruction an.description: Cecal volvulus is torsion of the cecum and terminal ileum, producing a closed-loop obstruction. The cecum may become markedly dilated and displaced, with risk of ischemia and perforation.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.normalized_text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) with colonic perforation
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.description: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is severe functional dilation of the colon without a mechanical blockage, usually in medically ill or immobilized patients. Extreme dilation can cause cecal ischemia and perforation.

Distal large-bowel obstruction from colo.normalized_text: Distal large-bowel obstruction from colorectal malignancy, complicated by perforation
Distal large-bowel obstruction from colo.description: An obstructing colorectal tumor can cause proximal colonic dilation and, when severe, ischemia or perforation. A competent ileocecal valve may create a closed-loop colonic obstruction.

Microscopic polyangiitis (ANCA-associate.normalized_text: Microscopic polyangiitis (ANCA-associated vasculitis) with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
Microscopic polyangiitis (ANCA-associate.description: A small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis, often associated with MPO/p-ANCA, that can cause pulmonary capillaritis with alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A PR3/c-ANCA-associated necrotizing granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis that may involve the lungs and kidneys, producing pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.

Leptospirosis with pulmonary hemorrhage.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira species that can produce fever, systemic inflammation, renal urinary abnormalities, and severe pulmonary capillary injury with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune disease caused by antibodies against the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, resulting in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

Hantavirus infection with pulmonary invo.description: A rodent-borne viral infection that can cause systemic inflammation, renal urinary abnormalities, capillary leak, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.

Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.normalized_text: Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome (HUVS) with renal involvement
Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.description: A systemic immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis strongly associated with anti-C1q antibodies and consumption of complement. Renal disease may present as immune-complex glomerulonephritis, often with membranoproliferative, proliferative, crescentic, or thrombotic microangiopathy-like features.

Lupus nephritis.description: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis caused by systemic lupus erythematosus. It commonly causes a "full-house" pattern on immunofluorescence and may produce proliferative glomerular injury, proteinuria, hematuria, nephrotic syndrome, and kidney dysfunction.

Immune-complex membranoproliferative glo.description: A pattern of glomerular injury caused by immune-complex deposition and complement activation. It can occur secondary to autoimmune disease, chronic infection, cryoglobulinemia, or hypocomplementemic vasculitis and often causes nephritic-nephrotic renal disease.

C1q nephropathy.description: An immune-complex glomerular disease characterized by dominant or codominant C1q deposition in the kidney in the absence of systemic lupus erythematosus. It may manifest with nephrotic syndrome, hematuria, and variable renal impairment.

Insufficient clinical information to det.normalized_text: Insufficient clinical information to determine a diagnosis
Insufficient clinical information to det.description: The provided images appear entirely black and contain no interpretable clinical findings, symptoms, examination details, or test results.

Clostridioides difficile infection (nons.description: Infection of the colon caused by toxin-producing Clostridioides difficile, typically presenting with diarrhea and abdominal symptoms, often after antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact. The normal white blood cell count and albumin are compatible with nonsevere disease if symptoms are present.

Asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile co.description: Presence of Clostridioides difficile in the intestine without active toxin-mediated colitis or clinically significant diarrhea. PCR can remain positive in colonized individuals because it detects organism genetic material rather than proving active symptomatic infection.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhea with inci.normalized_text: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea with incidental Clostridioides difficile PCR positivity
Antibiotic-associated diarrhea with inci.description: Diarrhea related to recent antibiotic use can occur without active C. difficile colitis. A positive PCR may represent colonization rather than the cause of symptoms, and confirmation of clinically significant diarrhea and toxin-mediated disease is needed.

Histoplasmosis diseminada.description: Infección sistémica con Histoplasma capsulatum, que ocurre principalmente en VIH/SIDA avanzado y que a menudo afecta a los pulmones, médula ósea, sistema reticuloendotelial, ganglios linfáticos y tracto gastrointestinal.

Tuberculosis miliar con tuberculosis ext.normalized_text: Tuberculosis miliar con tuberculosis extrapulmonar diseminada
Tuberculosis miliar con tuberculosis ext.description: Diseminación hematógena de Mycobacterium tuberculosis que produce innumerables nódulos pulmonares diminutos y posible afectación ganglionada, gastrointestinal, médula ósea y sistémica, especialmente en inmunosupresión severa.

Infección diseminada del complejo Mycoba.normalized_text: Infección diseminada del complejo Mycobacterium avium
Infección diseminada del complejo Mycoba.description: Una infección oportunista diseminada causada por el complejo Mycobacterium avium, que suele ocurrir en SIDA avanzado no tratado con recuentos CD4 inferiores a 50/mm³ y que a menudo provoca afectación de la médula, hígado, bazo y ganglios linfáticos.

Neumonía por Pneumocystis jirovecii.description: Una neumonía fúngica oportunista en pacientes con inmunodeficiencia celular severa, que clásicamente causa infiltraciones pulmonares bilaterales difusas en vidrio pulido y enfermedad respiratoria hipoxémica.

Linfoma asociado al VIH, incluyendo linf.normalized_text: Linfoma asociado al VIH, incluyendo linfoma no Hodgkin
Linfoma asociado al VIH, incluyendo linf.description: Los linfomas agresivos de células B son más comunes en el VIH avanzado y pueden afectar ganglios linfáticos, médula ósea, órganos gastrointestinales y pulmones, produciendo citopenias, LDH elevada y adenopatía.

HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/.normalized_text: HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), cutaneous type
HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/.description: A mature peripheral T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection. The cutaneous form can present predominantly with papules, plaques, scaling, erythroderma, or diffuse infiltrative skin lesions, with epidermotropic atypical T cells on biopsy.

Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymp.description: The most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, usually presenting with chronic patches, plaques, scaling, pigmentary change, and epidermotropism of atypical T lymphocytes on skin biopsy.

Sezary syndrome.description: An aggressive leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by erythroderma, severe pruritus, lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells with skin epidermotropism.

Chronic kidney disease-associated prurit.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus with xerosis (uremic dermatosis)
Chronic kidney disease-associated prurit.description: Advanced chronic kidney disease can cause severe dry, scaly skin, pruritus, excoriations, pigmentary changes, anemia of chronic disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, and iron-restricted erythropoiesis.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive autoimmune myocarditis characterized histologically by diffuse myocardial inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, myocyte necrosis, ventricular arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and often severe heart failure.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: An infiltrative granulomatous inflammatory disease of the heart that can cause conduction block, ventricular tachycardia, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. Histology usually shows noncaseating granulomas rather than diffuse giant-cell myocarditis.

Lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle, commonly viral or immune-mediated, which may cause chest pain, reduced cardiac function, arrhythmias, and occasionally ventricular tachycardia.

Postoperative wound dehiscence.description: Separation of a previously closed surgical incision, ranging from superficial skin separation to deeper fascial disruption.

Surgical site infection.description: Infection involving a surgical incision, which can cause inflammation, drainage, tissue breakdown, and delayed healing.

Infected wound with partial skin necrosi.normalized_text: Infected wound with partial skin necrosis
Infected wound with partial skin necrosi.description: Breakdown of skin and subcutaneous tissue in a wound, often associated with impaired blood supply, infection, tension on the incision, or poor healing conditions.

Abdominal wound healing by secondary int.normalized_text: Abdominal wound healing by secondary intention
Abdominal wound healing by secondary int.description: An open wound that is allowed to heal gradually from the base upward through granulation, contraction, and epithelialization, often after dehiscence or infection.

Zenker diverticulum.description: A pulsion diverticulum arising posteriorly at the pharyngoesophageal junction, usually due to impaired relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle.

Cricopharyngeal dysfunction (cricopharyn.description: Impaired opening or hypertrophy of the upper esophageal sphincter that can produce a posterior indentation and narrowing at the level of the cervical esophagus during swallowing.

Cervical esophageal web.description: A thin mucosal membrane in the proximal esophagus that causes a focal narrowing and may impair passage of swallowed contrast or solid food.

Giant pulmonary bulla (giant bullous emp.description: A very large air-filled space within the lung caused by destruction and coalescence of alveoli, which can compress adjacent normal lung and shift mediastinal structures.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening accumulation of pleural air under pressure that collapses the lung and can shift the mediastinum, impairing venous return and breathing.

Congenital lobar emphysema / congenital.normalized_text: Congenital lobar emphysema / congenital pulmonary airway abnormality with hyperinflation
Congenital lobar emphysema / congenital.description: A congenital lung abnormality that can cause severe overexpansion of a lung lobe or cystic air-filled spaces, compressing surrounding lung and mediastinal structures.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.normalized_text: Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (PBMAH) causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: A disorder of bilateral adrenal enlargement with multiple nodules that autonomously produce cortisol, resulting in ACTH-independent hypercortisolism. It commonly presents later in adulthood.

ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to.normalized_text: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to a cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to.description: A benign adrenal cortical tumor may autonomously secrete cortisol, suppressing pituitary ACTH and causing Cushing syndrome. Usually unilateral, although an incidental nodule may be present in the opposite adrenal gland.

Adrenocortical carcinoma with cortisol s.description: A malignant adrenal cortical neoplasm that can produce cortisol and cause ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. It more often appears as a large, heterogeneous unilateral adrenal mass and may produce other adrenal steroids.

Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical.description: A rare cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome characterized by multiple small adrenal cortical nodules, often associated with Carney complex and typically presenting in younger individuals.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Nephrotic syndrome due to primary membra.normalized_text: Nephrotic syndrome due to primary membranous nephropathy
Nephrotic syndrome due to primary membra.description: A glomerular disease causing heavy urinary protein loss, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and a marked tendency toward venous thrombosis, particularly renal-vein thrombosis.

Lupus nephritis associated with systemic.normalized_text: Lupus nephritis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus
Lupus nephritis associated with systemic.description: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis caused by systemic lupus erythematosus; it can produce proteinuria, hematuria, hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome, and thrombotic complications.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder causing arterial or venous thrombosis; it may occur alone or in association with systemic lupus erythematosus and can involve renal vessels.

Minimal change disease causing nephrotic.normalized_text: Minimal change disease causing nephrotic syndrome
Minimal change disease causing nephrotic.description: A podocyte disorder that causes abrupt heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and sometimes hypercoagulability; kidney function may initially remain normal.

Acute viral hepatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the liver caused by hepatotropic viruses, often producing periportal edema, gallbladder wall edema, and sometimes splenomegaly.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to cystic duct obstruction by gallstones, causing gallbladder wall thickening, distention, and pericholecystic inflammation.

Portal hypertension.description: Elevated pressure in the portal venous system, commonly related to chronic liver disease, portal vein obstruction, or splenic venous disease; it may cause splenomegaly, ascites, and congestive gallbladder wall thickening.

Systemic edema or venous congestion caus.normalized_text: Systemic edema or venous congestion causing secondary gallbladder wall edema
Systemic edema or venous congestion caus.description: Gallbladder wall thickening can occur secondarily from systemic conditions such as heart failure, renal failure, hypoalbuminemia, or generalized inflammatory states rather than primary gallbladder disease.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects renal, mesenteric, hepatic, and other visceral arteries, producing arterial stenoses, microaneurysms, thrombosis, and renal infarctions.

Segmental arterial mediolysis.description: A rare noninflammatory arteriopathy of medium-sized abdominal arteries characterized by arterial wall degeneration, dissections, aneurysms, stenoses, thrombosis, and organ ischemia or infarction.

Fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arteriopathy that most often affects renal and carotid arteries and may produce a characteristic string-of-beads appearance, stenosis, aneurysm, or dissection.

IgG4-related disease with inflammatory a.normalized_text: IgG4-related disease with inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm and retroperitoneal fibrosis
IgG4-related disease with inflammatory a.description: A systemic fibroinflammatory immune-mediated disease that can cause aortitis/periaortitis, inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm, retroperitoneal fibrosis with ureteral obstruction, and progressive renal impairment.

Behçet disease with vascular involvement.description: A multisystem vasculitis that can cause arterial aneurysms, thrombosis, gastrointestinal ulceration, pulmonary vascular lesions, and renal injury secondary to vascular or inflammatory complications.

Tuberculous aortitis with mycotic abdomi.normalized_text: Tuberculous aortitis with mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm and intestinal tuberculosis
Tuberculous aortitis with mycotic abdomi.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can rarely infect the aortic wall, producing a mycotic aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, and can also cause pulmonary and ileocecal gastrointestinal disease with systemic inflammation.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that may produce renal ischemia, hypertension, abdominal pain or bowel ischemia, mesenteric vascular abnormalities, aneurysms, and high inflammatory markers.

Infectious aortitis due to bacterial inf.normalized_text: Infectious aortitis due to bacterial infection (for example Salmonella or Staphylococcus) with infected abdominal aortic aneurysm
Infectious aortitis due to bacterial inf.description: Bacterial infection of the aortic wall can cause rapidly progressive inflammatory aneurysm formation, periaortic soft-tissue inflammation, systemic inflammatory response, and downstream organ dysfunction.

Hepatic bartonellosis (hepatosplenic cat.description: Disseminated infection with Bartonella henselae that can cause granulomatous hepatitis or hepatic inflammatory masses, often accompanied by erythema nodosum.

Hepatic tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the liver can produce granulomas, focal hepatic lesions, and systemic inflammatory manifestations including erythema nodosum.

Hepatic brucellosis.description: Brucella infection can cause granulomatous hepatitis, hepatic abscess-like lesions, and reactive skin manifestations such as erythema nodosum.

Sarcoidosis with hepatic involvement.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that may involve the liver and skin; erythema nodosum is a classic cutaneous manifestation.

Yersinia infection with granulomatous he.description: Yersinia enterocolitica or Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection can cause suppurative granulomas in the liver and can trigger erythema nodosum.

Sinus pericranii.description: A rare venous anomaly in which extracranial scalp veins communicate directly with intracranial dural venous sinuses through transcalvarial channels, often producing prominent scalp venous vessels.

Scalp arteriovenous malformation (cirsoi.description: An abnormal high-flow connection between scalp arteries and veins, producing dilated, tortuous superficial vessels and sometimes a pulsatile scalp mass.

Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.normalized_text: Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortical or extracranial venous drainage
Dural arteriovenous fistula with cortica.description: An acquired abnormal shunt between meningeal arteries and dural venous sinuses or cortical veins that can cause enlarged dural, cortical, transosseous, or scalp veins.

Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH).description: A benign hyperplastic liver lesion, often occurring in otherwise normal livers. It is typically hypervascular and may contain a central fibrous scar with radiating vessels.

Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A distinct subtype of hepatocellular carcinoma that often affects younger patients without cirrhosis and can appear as a large hepatic mass with a central fibrous scar.

Hepatocellular adenoma.description: A benign hepatocellular neoplasm, often associated with estrogen exposure, anabolic steroid use, obesity, or metabolic disease. It may be hypervascular and can become large.

Conventional hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes, most commonly arising in cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis. It often demonstrates arterial hyperenhancement and later washout.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare systemic histiocytic disorder characterized by destructive erosive polyarthritis and multiple reddish-brown papules or nodules, often involving the hands, periungual regions, and face.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, producing tophi, chronic inflammation, erosive arthritis, and deformity.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that can cause symmetric joint swelling, progressive deformity, and subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, especially in longstanding seropositive disease.

Psoriatic arthritis, mutilans subtype.description: A seronegative inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis that may cause dactylitis, nail changes, erosive joint disease, and severe arthritis mutilans with shortening or deformity of digits.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiom.description: An inherited cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement of right ventricular myocardium, causing ventricular arrhythmias and characteristic ECG abnormalities including epsilon waves and anterior T-wave inversion.

Brugada syndrome.description: An inherited cardiac sodium-channel disorder associated with risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death; ECG changes are most prominent in V1-V3.

Right ventricular conduction delay or in.normalized_text: Right ventricular conduction delay or incomplete right bundle branch block
Right ventricular conduction delay or in.description: Delayed conduction through the right ventricle can produce terminal QRS notching or an rSr' morphology in the right precordial leads.

Cardiac sarcoidosis with right ventricul.normalized_text: Cardiac sarcoidosis with right ventricular involvement
Cardiac sarcoidosis with right ventricul.description: Inflammatory granulomatous infiltration of the myocardium can cause conduction abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, scar-related ECG changes, and occasionally findings resembling ARVC.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An inherited vascular-malformation disorder characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, especially in the lungs, brain, liver, and gastrointestinal tract.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (P.description: Abnormal direct communications between pulmonary arteries and veins that create right-to-left shunting; they may occur alone but are commonly associated with HHT.

Cerebral arteriovenous malformations or.normalized_text: Cerebral arteriovenous malformations or cerebral capillary malformations associated with HHT
Cerebral arteriovenous malformations or.description: Congenital abnormal intracranial vascular connections or capillary vascular lesions that can occur as multiple enhancing brain lesions in patients with HHT.

Capillary malformation-arteriovenous mal.normalized_text: Capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation syndrome (CM-AVM; RASA1- or EPHB4-related disorder)
Capillary malformation-arteriovenous mal.description: A genetic vascular-malformation syndrome that may produce multifocal capillary malformations and fast-flow arteriovenous malformations involving the brain, lungs, skin, or other organs.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis with.description: A chronic destructive renal infection, usually associated with obstruction and recurrent infection, in which the kidney is replaced by inflammatory tissue containing foamy macrophages. Severe disease can extend into adjacent bowel and form a fistula.

Renal cell carcinoma invading the duoden.normalized_text: Renal cell carcinoma invading the duodenum
Renal cell carcinoma invading the duoden.description: A malignant kidney tumor that can directly invade neighboring structures, including the duodenum, and may cause ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, or fistula formation.

Renal abscess or chronic pyelonephritis.normalized_text: Renal abscess or chronic pyelonephritis with fistulization into the duodenum
Renal abscess or chronic pyelonephritis.description: A severe kidney infection can produce an abscess or chronically inflamed kidney and, rarely, erode into adjacent bowel to create a renoduodenal fistula.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-a.normalized_text: Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-associated arterial thromboembolism (Trousseau syndrome)
Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-a.description: Gastric adenocarcinoma can create a hypercoagulable state, causing arterial thrombosis or emboli and acute distal limb ischemia, including blue or gangrenous toes.

Acute limb ischemia due to arterial thro.normalized_text: Acute limb ischemia due to arterial thromboembolism
Acute limb ischemia due to arterial thro.description: Acute limb ischemia is sudden reduction of arterial blood flow to an extremity, often caused by embolus or thrombosis, leading to pain, cyanosis, tissue necrosis, and possible gangrene.

Blue toe syndrome.description: Blue toe syndrome is digital ischemia caused by occlusion of small arteries, commonly from cholesterol emboli, thromboemboli, or malignancy-related hypercoagulability; pulses may remain present in larger vessels.

Peripheral arterial disease with critica.normalized_text: Peripheral arterial disease with critical limb-threatening ischemia
Peripheral arterial disease with critica.description: Peripheral arterial disease results from atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion of lower-extremity arteries. Severe disease can cause chronic ischemia, ulceration, gangrene, and need for revascularization or amputation.

Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy) involving the prostate
Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A rare non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder characterized by infiltrates of large S100-positive histiocytes, often showing emperipolesis (intact inflammatory cells within histiocytes). It can occur at extranodal sites, including the genitourinary tract.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal histiocytic neoplasm composed of Langerhans cells, typically expressing CD1a, langerin (CD207), and S100. It may involve bone, skin, lungs, lymph nodes, and rarely the genitourinary tract.

Erdheim-Chester disease.description: A rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis caused by infiltration of tissues by lipid-laden foamy histiocytes, commonly associated with symmetric long-bone osteosclerosis and retroperitoneal, cardiovascular, or central nervous system involvement.

Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or.normalized_text: Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma
Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or.description: A benign ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma associated with ascites and pleural effusion, classically right-sided; fluid usually resolves after removal of the ovarian tumor.

Pseudo-Meigs syndrome from uterine leiom.description: A syndrome of ascites and pleural effusion caused by a benign pelvic tumor other than ovarian fibroma, commonly a large uterine leiomyoma.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with malign.normalized_text: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with malignant ascites and pleural effusion
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with malign.description: A malignant ovarian tumor that can spread within the peritoneum, causing ascites, pelvic masses, and pleural effusions; pleural involvement may indicate advanced-stage disease.

Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor, such as.normalized_text: Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor, such as thecoma or granulosa-cell tumor
Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor, such as.description: Ovarian tumors arising from sex cord-stromal tissue that may present as a pelvic mass; fibrothecoma variants can produce ascites and pleural effusion resembling Meigs syndrome.

Cervical tuberculous spondylitis (Pott d.normalized_text: Cervical tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with prevertebral/retropharyngeal abscess and possible tuberculous meningitis
Cervical tuberculous spondylitis (Pott d.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine can cause multilevel vertebral marrow involvement, paravertebral or prevertebral abscesses, epidural extension, and, when disseminated, meningeal inflammation in the brain.

Pyogenic cervical spondylodiscitis with.normalized_text: Pyogenic cervical spondylodiscitis with retropharyngeal abscess
Pyogenic cervical spondylodiscitis with.description: Bacterial infection of cervical vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs may produce vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, prevertebral phlegmon or abscess, and possible epidural extension.

Cervical spinal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can infiltrate vertebral marrow and form epidural, paravertebral, or prevertebral soft-tissue masses, often with relatively preserved disc spaces.

Metastatic malignancy involving the cerv.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the cervical spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the cerv.description: Metastatic cancer may involve multiple vertebral bodies and extend into paraspinal or epidural soft tissues, potentially causing spinal cord compression.

Fungal vertebral osteomyelitis with para.normalized_text: Fungal vertebral osteomyelitis with paravertebral abscess
Fungal vertebral osteomyelitis with para.description: Fungal infections, especially in immunocompromised patients, can cause vertebral osteomyelitis with paraspinal or prevertebral abscesses and may disseminate to the central nervous system.

Diffuse plexiform neurofibroma.description: A benign peripheral-nerve-sheath tumor, often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, that can diffusely infiltrate skin, subcutaneous tissue, and deeper soft tissues. It may produce a plaque-like lesion with overlying hyperpigmentation and excess hair.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign congenital skin hamartoma caused by excessive, disorganized bundles of smooth muscle, usually arrector pili muscle. It commonly presents as a hyperpigmented and hairy patch or plaque on the trunk or lumbosacral region.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A rare benign fibroblastic and fatty soft-tissue tumor occurring mainly in infants and young children. It often affects the upper trunk, axilla, shoulder, or inguinal region and may extend from the dermis into subcutaneous tissue.

Williams-Campbell syndrome.description: A rare congenital deficiency of cartilage in subsegmental bronchi, causing distal airway collapse and diffuse bilateral cystic bronchiectasis, often with recurrent respiratory infections.

Cystic fibrosis with bronchiectasis.description: An inherited CFTR disorder causing dehydrated airway secretions, recurrent infection, mucus impaction, and typically upper-lobe-predominant bronchiectasis.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia.description: A genetic disorder of impaired mucociliary clearance that causes chronic sinus and lower respiratory infections, resulting in bronchiectasis; some patients have situs inversus.

Postinfectious bronchiectasis.description: Permanent bronchial dilatation caused by prior severe or recurrent pulmonary infections, including bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, or childhood lower respiratory tract infection.

Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast.normalized_text: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast
Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast.description: The most common type of invasive breast cancer, arising from mammary ducts and growing into surrounding breast tissue; it often appears as an irregular hypoechoic mass with suspicious enhancement on MRI.

Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast.normalized_text: Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast
Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast.description: A malignant breast tumor arising from lobules that may be difficult to identify on mammography, particularly in dense breasts, and can present as an infiltrative or enhancing mass on MRI.

Phyllodes tumor.description: A fibroepithelial breast tumor that can be benign, borderline, or malignant and often presents as a rapidly enlarging, relatively large breast mass with heterogeneous ultrasound and MRI appearances.

Fibroadenoma.description: A common benign fibroepithelial breast lesion, usually presenting as a well-defined solid mass; some fibroadenomas can enhance on MRI and may be difficult to characterize in dense breasts.

Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZ.description: An outer-retinal disorder, often affecting young myopic women, characterized by acute photopsias and visual-field loss with initially subtle or normal-appearing fundus findings. It may produce zonal retinal pigment epithelium changes on fluorescein angiography.

Autoimmune retinopathy.description: An immune-mediated retinal degeneration, sometimes associated with cancer and sometimes idiopathic, that causes progressive photoreceptor dysfunction, visual-field constriction or ring scotomas, and initially subtle retinal findings.

Early retinitis pigmentosa or retinitis.normalized_text: Early retinitis pigmentosa or retinitis pigmentosa sine pigmento
Early retinitis pigmentosa or retinitis.description: An inherited retinal degeneration involving rod photoreceptors first, causing night blindness, progressive peripheral field loss, and eventually ring scotomas and characteristic pigmentary retinal changes. Early disease may lack obvious bone-spicule pigmentation.

Cone-rod dystrophy.description: A hereditary or sporadic photoreceptor dystrophy in which cone dysfunction, followed by rod dysfunction, produces central visual impairment, dyschromatopsia, photophobia, and progressive visual-field defects that may become annular.

Acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement.normalized_text: Acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement syndrome (AIBSE)
Acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement.description: An outer-retinal inflammatory syndrome causing enlargement of the physiologic blind spot, often with photopsias and little or no visible retinal abnormality. It overlaps clinically with the AZOOR spectrum.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mixed cellul.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mixed cellularity subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mixed cellul.description: A subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by scattered Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background. Reed-Sternberg cells typically express CD30 and CD15.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: The most common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, typically showing lacunar-type Reed-Sternberg cells, CD30 and CD15 positivity, and fibrous bands that divide the tissue into nodules.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma with large pleomorphic malignant cells that can resemble Reed-Sternberg cells. It is generally negative for CD15 and often expresses T-cell markers and, in some cases, ALK.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Inflammatory granulomatous involvement of the heart, often associated with thoracic lymph-node or pulmonary sarcoidosis. It can cause focal myocardial inflammation, ventricular dysfunction or aneurysm, arrhythmias, and conduction abnormalities.

Ischemic cardiomyopathy with left ventri.normalized_text: Ischemic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular aneurysm
Ischemic cardiomyopathy with left ventri.description: Myocardial scarring and impaired ventricular function caused by prior coronary artery ischemia or infarction; a chronically infarcted segment can form a ventricular aneurysm.

Myocarditis, including giant-cell myocar.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle that may cause focal FDG uptake, reduced ventricular contractility, arrhythmias, and occasionally ventricular dilation or aneurysmal change.

Chagas cardiomyopathy.description: Chronic cardiac disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection, characterized by conduction disease, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, and classically an apical left ventricular aneurysm.

Chronic endometritis.description: Persistent inflammation of the endometrial lining, characterized histologically by stromal plasma cells, often highlighted by CD138 immunostaining.

Acute endometritis.description: Acute infection or inflammation of the endometrium, usually marked by neutrophils infiltrating endometrial glands and stroma; it may occur postpartum, after instrumentation, or with ascending genital-tract infection.

Pelvic inflammatory disease with endomet.normalized_text: Pelvic inflammatory disease with endometrial involvement
Pelvic inflammatory disease with endomet.description: An ascending infection of the female genital tract that may involve the endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and surrounding pelvic structures. Endometrial biopsy can show acute or chronic endometritis.

Endometrial polyp with secondary chronic.normalized_text: Endometrial polyp with secondary chronic inflammation
Endometrial polyp with secondary chronic.description: A localized benign overgrowth of endometrial glands and stroma that can develop chronic inflammatory changes, particularly if irritated, infarcted, or infected.

Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria.description: Presence of a small amount of blood in urine detectable on dipstick without visible red urine or other urinary symptoms. It can be transient or require confirmation with urine microscopy.

Transient benign hematuria (for example.normalized_text: Transient benign hematuria (for example after exercise, minor trauma, dehydration, or recent illness)
Transient benign hematuria (for example.description: Temporary blood detected in urine that may occur after vigorous exercise, mild trauma, fever, or other short-lived physiologic stressors and often resolves on repeat testing.

Nephrolithiasis (kidney or ureteral ston.description: Mineral stones in the kidney or urinary tract can irritate the lining of the urinary system and cause microscopic or visible blood in urine.

Glomerular kidney disease.description: Diseases affecting the kidney filtering units, such as glomerulonephritis or IgA nephropathy, may cause microscopic hematuria and can sometimes initially have few symptoms.

Urinary tract infection.description: An infection of the bladder or urinary tract can cause blood in urine, typically accompanied by inflammatory urine findings and urinary discomfort.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an F.normalized_text: Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an FGG gene variant
Congenital dysfibrinogenemia due to an F.description: An inherited qualitative fibrinogen disorder caused by variants in fibrinogen genes, commonly FGG. The sequencing image is consistent with evaluation for a fibrinogen-gene sequence variant. Dysfibrinogenemia may cause abnormal clotting tests and can be asymptomatic or associated with bleeding or thrombosis.

Factor XII deficiency.description: Factor XII deficiency is an inherited or acquired coagulation-factor deficiency that can prolong laboratory clotting assays, especially the activated partial thromboplastin time, but usually does not cause clinical bleeding.

Lupus anticoagulant or another nonspecif.normalized_text: Lupus anticoagulant or another nonspecific coagulation inhibitor
Lupus anticoagulant or another nonspecif.description: Lupus anticoagulant is an antiphospholipid antibody that interferes with phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays. It often produces incomplete correction in mixing studies and may be associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding.

Acute-phase or endothelial-activation st.normalized_text: Acute-phase or endothelial-activation state causing elevated von Willebrand factor
Acute-phase or endothelial-activation st.description: Von Willebrand factor is an acute-phase reactant and may become substantially elevated with inflammation, infection, physiologic stress, endothelial injury, pregnancy, liver disease, or thrombotic states. Elevated VWF can be a marker of increased thrombotic risk rather than a bleeding disorder.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung

Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with.normalized_text: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with mediastinal invasion and esophageal perforation/fistula
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with.description: A malignant squamous tumor of the esophagus that can ulcerate, invade adjacent mediastinal structures, cause fistulization or perforation, and lead to mediastinal infection or abscess formation. The endoscopic lesion, malignant-appearing histology, mediastinal mass, and FDG-avid disease support this possibility.

Primary lung squamous cell carcinoma wit.normalized_text: Primary lung squamous cell carcinoma with mediastinal extension and esophageal involvement
Primary lung squamous cell carcinoma wit.description: A centrally located non-small-cell lung cancer, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, may invade the mediastinum and esophagus, producing extrinsic compression, ulceration, fistula, mediastinitis, and adrenal metastasis.

Mediastinal abscess/descending necrotizi.normalized_text: Mediastinal abscess/descending necrotizing mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
Mediastinal abscess/descending necrotizi.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum caused by contamination from an esophageal perforation, fistula, or nearby infection. CT may show mediastinal fluid, inflammatory soft tissue, gas, and extension into the neck or chest wall; treatment often requires drainage plus broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy.

Mediastinal lymphoma with esophageal com.normalized_text: Mediastinal lymphoma with esophageal compression or invasion
Mediastinal lymphoma with esophageal com.description: Lymphoma can present as an FDG-avid mediastinal mass and may cause esophageal compression, systemic inflammation, anemia, and hypoalbuminemia. Tissue diagnosis is required because it can mimic carcinoma or infection on imaging.

Transient T-cell lymphopenia of infancy.description: A temporary reduction in T-cell number and/or thymic output detected in infancy, sometimes identified through newborn screening with absent or low TRECs, that later normalizes.

Partial DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 delet.normalized_text: Partial DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome with thymic hypoplasia)
Partial DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 delet.description: A chromosomal disorder that can cause variable thymic hypoplasia and neonatal T-cell lymphopenia, often with relatively preserved B-cell and NK-cell numbers. T-cell immunity may improve over time in partial forms.

Cornelia de Lange syndrome.description: A developmental genetic syndrome characterized by distinctive craniofacial features, excessive body hair, growth and developmental abnormalities, and occasionally immune abnormalities including reduced T-cell subsets.

Kabuki syndrome.description: A multisystem genetic disorder with characteristic facial features, developmental abnormalities, and variable immune dysfunction that may include T-cell abnormalities, impaired vaccine responses, or hypogammaglobulinemia.

CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia.description: A genetic developmental syndrome that may include thymic hypoplasia and T-cell lymphopenia, especially in infancy; immune severity ranges from mild transient lymphopenia to significant combined immunodeficiency.

Coffin-Siris syndrome.description: A chromatin-remodeling disorder associated with coarse or distinctive facial appearance, excessive body hair, developmental delay, and occasionally recurrent infections or immune abnormalities.

Human intestinal spirochetosis.description: Colonization or infection of the colonic mucosal surface by Brachyspira species, classically producing a basophilic 'false brush border' on histology and positive spirochete immunostaining.

Infectious colitis.description: Inflammation of the colon caused by an infectious organism, including bacterial, parasitic, viral, or spirochetal pathogens.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, usually beginning in the rectum.

Ischemic colitis.description: Acute colonic injury caused by reduced blood flow, often producing edematous, erythematous, dusky, or violaceous mucosa with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding.

Ovarian vein thrombosis with pulmonary e.normalized_text: Ovarian vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
Ovarian vein thrombosis with pulmonary e.description: Thrombosis of an ovarian vein, often occurring postpartum or in association with pelvic infection, surgery, malignancy, or hypercoagulable states; the clot can embolize to the pulmonary arteries.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, most commonly originating from deep veins of the legs or pelvis.

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.description: Inflammatory thrombosis of pelvic veins, commonly involving the ovarian vein, usually associated with postpartum uterine infection, pelvic surgery, or pelvic inflammatory infection.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.description: An inherited phagocyte disorder, most commonly caused by CYBB mutations affecting gp91phox, resulting in defective NADPH oxidase activity and failure of neutrophils to generate an oxidative burst.

Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatou.description: A form of CGD caused by defects in other NADPH oxidase complex components, such as NCF1, NCF2, NCF4, or CYBA, leading to impaired neutrophil killing of catalase-positive organisms.

Myeloperoxidase deficiency.description: A neutrophil enzyme deficiency that can produce an abnormal oxidation-dependent flow-cytometry assay; most affected people are asymptomatic, although some may develop severe Candida infections.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary bile-duct cancer arising within the liver, usually forming a fibrous, gland-producing adenocarcinoma. It may present as a solitary mass or multifocal intrahepatic lesions.

Metastatic adenocarcinoma to the liver.description: Cancer spread to the liver from a gland-forming primary tumor elsewhere, commonly colorectal, pancreatic, gastric, breast, lung, or biliary tract adenocarcinoma.

Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcino.description: A rare primary liver malignancy showing mixed hepatocellular and biliary epithelial differentiation. Imaging can overlap with hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.

Hepatic metastases from colorectal adeno.description: Colorectal cancer commonly spreads to the liver and often produces multiple diffusion-restricting lesions with peripheral or target-like enhancement; pathology typically shows gland-forming adenocarcinoma.

Cervical vagal schwannoma.description: A benign, slow-growing peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising from Schwann cells of the vagus nerve, often presenting as a deep neck or parapharyngeal-space mass.

Cervical sympathetic chain schwannoma.description: A benign schwannoma originating from the cervical sympathetic chain, typically producing a painless lateral neck or parapharyngeal mass and potentially causing postoperative Horner syndrome if the sympathetic chain is affected.

Cellular schwannoma.description: A histologic variant of schwannoma characterized by densely cellular fascicles of spindle cells, often with less prominent Antoni B areas and sometimes mimicking a malignant spindle-cell tumor.

Neurofibroma.description: A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and other nerve elements; unlike schwannoma, it more often infiltrates the parent nerve rather than being encapsulated.

Solitary fibrous tumor.description: A usually benign mesenchymal spindle-cell neoplasm that can occur in the head and neck and typically shows a patternless architecture with branching vessels and STAT6/CD34 positivity.

Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL).description: White-matter injury, most often related to prematurity or perinatal hypoxic-ischemic insult, characterized by periventricular gliosis, white-matter volume loss, and ventricular enlargement or irregularity.

Chronic hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Chronic brain injury following reduced oxygen delivery or cerebral perfusion around birth; in preterm infants it commonly produces a periventricular white-matter injury pattern.

Leukodystrophy or inherited white-matter.description: A broad group of genetic disorders causing abnormal myelin formation or progressive white-matter degeneration, often producing bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR white-matter hyperintensity.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Laryngomalacia.description: A congenital dynamic collapse of supraglottic laryngeal structures during inspiration, commonly involving an omega-shaped epiglottis, shortened aryepiglottic folds, and prolapsing arytenoid mucosa.

Bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Impaired movement of both vocal folds, often leaving them near the midline and causing a small glottic airway; it may produce significant airway obstruction and inspiratory stridor.

Posterior glottic stenosis.description: Scar-related narrowing of the posterior glottis, frequently following prolonged intubation or laryngeal injury, which can restrict vocal-fold abduction and reduce the airway opening.

Congenital laryngeal web or glottic sten.normalized_text: Congenital laryngeal web or glottic stenosis
Congenital laryngeal web or glottic sten.description: A congenital membrane or fixed narrowing involving the glottis that reduces the airway aperture and may affect voice and breathing.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervica.normalized_text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervical lymph-node metastasis
Papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervica.description: A common differentiated thyroid cancer that may present as a thyroid or lower-neck mass; metastatic cervical nodes can contain punctate or coarse calcifications.

Calcified benign thyroid nodule (multino.normalized_text: Calcified benign thyroid nodule (multinodular goiter or thyroid adenoma)
Calcified benign thyroid nodule (multino.description: A noncancerous thyroid enlargement or discrete thyroid nodule that can become palpable and may develop dystrophic calcification over time.

Thyroid tuberculosis with abscess or sin.normalized_text: Thyroid tuberculosis with abscess or sinus formation
Thyroid tuberculosis with abscess or sin.description: A rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis involving the thyroid, which may cause a painful or painless neck mass, abscess, skin involvement, and calcification in chronic lesions.

Chronic suppurative thyroiditis or thyro.normalized_text: Chronic suppurative thyroiditis or thyroid abscess
Chronic suppurative thyroiditis or thyro.description: Bacterial infection of the thyroid causing inflammatory enlargement, abscess formation, and occasionally extension toward the skin; chronic inflammation can occasionally calcify.

Acute urticaria (hives).description: A transient hypersensitivity skin reaction producing pruritic, pink-to-red wheals that may become annular or polycyclic and occur widely on the trunk and extremities.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A drug- or infection-associated immune reaction that commonly causes urticarial or annular skin lesions, often accompanied by fever, joint pain, and swelling.

Urticarial vasculitis.description: An inflammatory small-vessel disorder causing urticaria-like plaques that tend to persist longer than ordinary hives and may burn, hurt, or leave bruise-like discoloration.

Erythema multiforme.description: An immune-mediated eruption, often triggered by herpes simplex infection or medications, characterized by fixed target-like lesions that usually begin on the extremities and may spread to the trunk.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive annular erythema characterized by slowly expanding ring-shaped patches, sometimes with an inner trailing scale, commonly affecting the trunk and proximal limbs.

Gastric trichobezoar with Rapunzel syndr.description: A trichobezoar is a compact mass of swallowed hair retained in the stomach. Rapunzel syndrome occurs when the hair mass extends through the pylorus into the small intestine, potentially causing obstruction, inflammation, ulceration, or bleeding.

Gastric bezoar causing partial gastric o.normalized_text: Gastric bezoar causing partial gastric outlet or intestinal obstruction
Gastric bezoar causing partial gastric o.description: A gastric bezoar is an accumulation of indigestible material in the stomach that can obstruct gastric emptying or migrate into the intestine. Bezoars may consist of hair, plant fibers, medications, or other foreign material.

Phytobezoar.description: A phytobezoar is a mass of undigested vegetable or fruit fibers, often occurring in patients with impaired gastric motility, prior gastric surgery, poor mastication, or high-fiber intake. It may cause gastric or small-bowel obstruction.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the gastrointestinal tract, characterized by granulomatous inflammation that may show caseous necrosis and acid-fast bacilli.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial gastrointes.description: Infection of gastrointestinal tissue by mycobacterial species other than M. tuberculosis, which can produce granulomatous inflammation and acid-fast organisms, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause transmural intestinal inflammation and noncaseating granulomas.

Left ventricular hypertrophy with second.normalized_text: Left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary repolarization changes
Left ventricular hypertrophy with second.description: Increased left-ventricular muscle mass, commonly related to longstanding hypertension or aortic valve disease, producing high-voltage QRS complexes and possible ST-T wave changes.

Benign early repolarization pattern.description: A common nonischemic ECG variant, particularly in younger or otherwise healthy individuals, characterized by mild concave ST elevation and prominent T waves in precordial leads.

Anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial.description: Acute occlusion of a coronary artery supplying the anterior left ventricle, usually causing persistent ST elevation in anterior leads and often requiring urgent reperfusion treatment.

Incomplete right bundle branch block or.normalized_text: Incomplete right bundle branch block or nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay
Incomplete right bundle branch block or.description: Delayed conduction through the right bundle branch or ventricular conduction system, producing mild QRS widening and altered right-precordial QRS morphology.

Right-sided aortic arch.description: A congenital variant in which the aortic arch courses to the right of the trachea rather than the left. It may be isolated or associated with other vascular anomalies.

Aberrant left subclavian artery associat.normalized_text: Aberrant left subclavian artery associated with a right-sided aortic arch
Aberrant left subclavian artery associat.description: A congenital arch anomaly in which the left subclavian artery arises abnormally, often from a diverticulum of Kommerell, and may pass behind the esophagus or trachea.

Vascular ring due to right aortic arch w.normalized_text: Vascular ring due to right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery and left ligamentum arteriosum
Vascular ring due to right aortic arch w.description: A vascular ring is a congenital arrangement of the aortic arch and its branches that can partially or completely surround and compress the trachea and esophagus.

Double aortic arch.description: A congenital vascular ring in which right and left aortic arch components encircle the trachea and esophagus, potentially causing airway or swallowing compression.

Erythema migrans (Lyme disease).description: An expanding red skin lesion caused by Borrelia infection after a tick bite; it may appear as a uniform expanding patch or as a target-like rash with central clearing.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial fungal infection of the skin that commonly produces a circular or ring-shaped red lesion with a more active border and central clearing.

Bullous arthropod bite reaction.description: A pronounced local inflammatory reaction to an insect or arachnid bite that can cause redness, swelling, central blistering, or bruise-like color change.

Erythema multiforme.description: An immune-mediated skin eruption, often triggered by infections or medications, characterized by target-shaped lesions with concentric zones of color.

Fixed drug eruption.description: A medication-related skin reaction that produces one or more sharply defined red-to-violaceous patches, sometimes with a central blister or dusky appearance, recurring at the same site after re-exposure.

Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.description: An acute myocardial infarction syndrome in which coronary angiography shows no obstructive epicardial coronary artery stenosis; causes include plaque disruption, vasospasm, embolism, or microvascular dysfunction.

Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome due to plaque disruption
Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.description: Acute coronary ischemia caused by plaque rupture or plaque erosion with thrombosis that may be transient, partially recanalized, or not clearly visible on routine coronary angiography.

Coronary vasospastic angina (epicardial.description: Transient constriction of an epicardial coronary artery causing reversible myocardial ischemia; the coronary arteries may appear normal or only mildly diseased when angiography is performed outside an episode.

Coronary microvascular dysfunction (micr.description: Impaired vasodilation or abnormal constriction of the small coronary vessels causing myocardial ischemia despite absence of obstructive disease in the major epicardial coronary arteries.

Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.description: A TP63-related disorder characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformations, ectodermal abnormalities, dental agenesis or malformed teeth, and sometimes cleft lip or palate.

Split-hand/split-foot malformation with.description: A congenital limb-malformation disorder causing central ray deficiency, cleft hands or feet, oligodactyly, and variable syndactyly; it may occur with or without long-bone defects.

Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome.description: A TP63-related ectodermal dysplasia syndrome with hypodontia, abnormal teeth, sparse hair or nail changes, clefting, and variable hand or foot malformations including syndactyly.

Oculodentodigital dysplasia.description: A genetic disorder, usually caused by GJA1 variants, involving characteristic facial and eye findings, dental abnormalities, and hand/foot syndactyly or digital malformations.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: An intermittent supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. The Holter explicitly documents two episodes.

Frequent premature atrial contractions (.normalized_text: Frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs) / supraventricular ectopy
Frequent premature atrial contractions (.description: Premature beats arising from the atria outside the sinus node. A high PAC burden can cause palpitations and may trigger atrial tachyarrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation.

Nonsustained atrial tachycardia / suprav.description: A rapid rhythm originating above the ventricles, often seen on Holter monitoring as short runs of consecutive supraventricular beats. It can coexist with frequent PACs and atrial fibrillation.

Occasional premature ventricular contrac.description: Early beats originating in the ventricles. In this recording, the ventricular ectopic burden is low and there is no evidence of sustained ventricular tachycardia.

Gastric extranodal marginal zone lymphom.normalized_text: Gastric extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (gastric MALT lymphoma)
Gastric extranodal marginal zone lymphom.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma arising in gastric mucosa, commonly associated with chronic Helicobacter pylori infection. It may appear endoscopically as erythema, erosions, ulcers, enlarged folds, or mass-like lesions and histologically shows dense small B-cell infiltrates with lymphoepithelial lesions.

Helicobacter pylori-associated chronic a.normalized_text: Helicobacter pylori-associated chronic active gastritis with lymphoid follicle formation
Helicobacter pylori-associated chronic a.description: Chronic H. pylori infection causes gastric mucosal inflammation, erythema, erosions, ulceration, and prominent lymphoid aggregates or follicles. It is also the principal precursor condition for gastric MALT lymphoma.

Gastric adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the stomach that may present as an irregular ulcer, depressed lesion, mucosal discoloration, or infiltrative mass. Histology usually demonstrates dysplastic or invasive malignant gland-forming epithelial cells rather than a predominantly lymphoid infiltrate.

Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic.normalized_text: Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic stomach (gastrothorax)
Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic.description: A congenital defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal organs, commonly the stomach and bowel, to herniate into the chest. An intrathoracic gas-filled stomach can create a large air-fluid level and mimic a hydropneumothorax.

Hydropneumothorax.description: Hydropneumothorax is the presence of both air and fluid in the pleural space, producing a sharp horizontal air-fluid level with pleural air above and fluid below.

Tension gastrothorax due to diaphragmati.normalized_text: Tension gastrothorax due to diaphragmatic hernia
Tension gastrothorax due to diaphragmati.description: Tension gastrothorax occurs when a distended stomach herniates into the thorax and causes lung compression and mediastinal shift. It is a potentially life-threatening complication of congenital or acquired diaphragmatic hernia.

Acquired diaphragmatic hernia.description: An acquired diaphragmatic hernia may occur after blunt or penetrating trauma, surgery, or other diaphragmatic injury, allowing stomach or bowel to enter the thorax.

Complicated pleural empyema with pyopneu.description: Pyopneumothorax is a pleural-space infection containing pus and air, often caused by infection, bronchopleural fistula, or a procedure. It can produce a pleural air-fluid level and lung compression.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis (ty.description: A fibroinflammatory manifestation of IgG4-related disease causing pancreatic enlargement or mass-like lesions, dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform fibrosis, and increased IgG4-positive plasma cells. It can involve the kidneys and other organs.

IgG4-related kidney disease associated w.normalized_text: IgG4-related kidney disease associated with autoimmune pancreatitis
IgG4-related kidney disease associated w.description: Renal involvement in IgG4-related disease, most often tubulointerstitial nephritis or renal cortical lesions, occurring with pancreatic and other systemic IgG4-related manifestations.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreas that commonly presents as a pancreatic mass and may cause biliary obstruction, abdominal pain, weight loss, or metastatic disease.

Primary pancreatic lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the pancreas that can produce a pancreatic mass and may mimic pancreatic carcinoma or autoimmune pancreatitis on imaging.

Multidrug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoea.description: Gonorrhea caused by N. gonorrhoeae with resistance to multiple commonly used antibiotics, including ceftriaxone, penicillin G, and ciprofloxacin.

Ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhea.description: Gonorrhea caused by N. gonorrhoeae with resistance or markedly reduced susceptibility to ceftriaxone, an extended-spectrum cephalosporin commonly used as first-line treatment.

Fluoroquinolone-resistant gonorrhea.description: Gonorrhea caused by N. gonorrhoeae that is resistant to fluoroquinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, limiting use of this antibiotic class for treatment.

Giant bullous emphysema (vanishing lung.description: A severe form of emphysema in which large air-filled bullae form from destruction of lung tissue, sometimes occupying a substantial portion of a hemithorax and compressing adjacent lung.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) or congenital giant pulmonary bulla
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A congenital cystic or air-filled lung abnormality that can persist into adulthood and may appear as a large localized air-containing lesion, sometimes causing compression of surrounding lung.

Pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete collapse of the lung. A giant pulmonary bulla can mimic pneumothorax on chest radiography.

Erdheim-Chester disease.description: A rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterized by infiltrates of lipid-laden histiocytes, commonly causing symmetric long-bone involvement, perirenal soft-tissue infiltration ('hairy kidney'), and circumferential periaortic sheathing ('coated aorta').

IgG4-related disease with retroperitonea.description: A systemic immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder that can cause retroperitoneal fibrosis, periaortitis, renal involvement, and tissue infiltration by lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: A fibroinflammatory condition causing plaque-like retroperitoneal tissue, often surrounding the aorta and ureters and potentially leading to ureteral obstruction or hydronephrosis.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal histiocytic neoplasm composed of Langerhans cells, typically expressing CD1a and langerin/CD207; it can involve bone, skin, lungs, pituitary gland, and occasionally other organs.

Lymphocytic thrombophilic arteritis (mac.description: A chronic cutaneous small- to medium-vessel vasculopathy characterized by livedo racemosa or irregular hyperpigmented/violaceous macules. Biopsy typically shows a lymphocytic arteritis with a fibrin ring and luminal thrombosis.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis affecting small- and medium-sized arteries in the skin, often causing livedo racemosa, tender nodules, purpura, ulceration, and sometimes neuropathic symptoms.

Antiphospholipid syndrome with cutaneous.normalized_text: Antiphospholipid syndrome with cutaneous thrombotic vasculopathy
Antiphospholipid syndrome with cutaneous.description: An autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause arterial and venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy morbidity, and skin findings such as livedo racemosa, retiform purpura, and cutaneous necrosis.

Livedoid vasculopathy.description: A thrombotic occlusive disease of dermal blood vessels that produces livedoid or purpuric lesions, usually on the lower extremities, and may progress to painful ulcers and porcelain-white atrophic scars.

Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.normalized_text: Classical homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of transsulfuration causing markedly elevated homocysteine and methionine. It commonly produces ectopia lentis, marfanoid skeletal features, osteoporosis, and thromboembolic risk.

Marfan syndrome.description: A connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by pathogenic variants in FBN1, characterized by marfanoid body habitus, chest-wall deformity, skeletal abnormalities, and lens dislocation.

Remethylation disorder causing homocysti.normalized_text: Remethylation disorder causing homocystinuria (for example, MTHFR deficiency or cobalamin metabolism defect)
Remethylation disorder causing homocysti.description: Inherited defects of homocysteine remethylation can cause severe hyperhomocysteinemia, often with neurologic, developmental, hematologic, or thrombotic manifestations. Unlike CBS deficiency, methionine is usually low or normal.

Brainstem cavernous malformation (pontin.normalized_text: Brainstem cavernous malformation (pontine cavernoma) causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Brainstem cavernous malformation (pontin.description: A cavernous malformation is a cluster of abnormal, low-flow blood vessels that can bleed repeatedly. A lesion in the pons or dorsal brainstem can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow through the fourth ventricle or cerebral aqueduct, producing hydrocephalus.

Brainstem hemorrhage with intraventricul.normalized_text: Brainstem hemorrhage with intraventricular cerebrospinal-fluid obstruction
Brainstem hemorrhage with intraventricul.description: A small hemorrhage in the pons or adjacent fourth-ventricular region may obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and lead to acute or subacute obstructive hydrocephalus. Causes include hypertension, vascular malformation, or hemorrhagic tumor.

Fourth-ventricular/brainstem ependymoma.description: Ependymoma is a glial tumor that can arise from the lining of the fourth ventricle or nearby brainstem. It may obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow and cause enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T lymphocytes, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. Bone marrow may show hemophagocytosis.

Infection-associated hemophagocytic synd.description: A form of secondary HLH precipitated by severe infection, commonly viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus, but also bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections.

EBV-associated hemophagocytic lymphohist.description: A severe EBV-triggered hyperinflammatory disorder in which activated cytotoxic lymphocytes and macrophages cause cytokine excess, hemophagocytosis, liver injury, hyperferritinemia, and cytopenias.

Malignancy-associated hemophagocytic lym.normalized_text: Malignancy-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, especially lymphoma-associated HLH
Malignancy-associated hemophagocytic lym.description: Secondary HLH can be triggered by hematologic malignancy, particularly aggressive T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma, and may present with profound inflammatory activation, cytopenias, liver injury, and marrow hemophagocytosis.

Severe sepsis with sepsis-associated cyt.normalized_text: Severe sepsis with sepsis-associated cytopenias and macrophage activation
Severe sepsis with sepsis-associated cyt.description: Severe systemic infection can produce inflammation, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, liver injury, hypertriglyceridemia, and a macrophage-activation state that overlaps clinically and pathologically with secondary HLH.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Progressive jawbone necrosis associated with antiresorptive or antiangiogenic medications, often causing exposed devitalized bone, infection, fistulae, and pathologic fracture.

Chronic suppurative osteomyelitis of the.normalized_text: Chronic suppurative osteomyelitis of the maxilla and mandible
Chronic suppurative osteomyelitis of the.description: A persistent bacterial infection of bone causing inflammation, necrosis, sequestrum formation, osteolysis, fistulae, and possible pathologic fracture.

Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis with.description: An invasive fungal infection, usually in immunocompromised patients, that can rapidly invade the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, palate, orbit, and facial bones, causing tissue necrosis.

Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw.description: Delayed radiation-induced bone death caused by hypovascular, hypocellular tissue after head and neck radiotherapy; it may result in exposed bone, chronic ulceration, infection, and fracture.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma with invasi.normalized_text: Oral squamous cell carcinoma with invasion of the maxilla or mandible
Oral squamous cell carcinoma with invasi.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the oral cavity that can present as a persistent ulcer and invade adjacent jawbone, producing destructive osteolytic changes and fracture in advanced disease.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Inflammatory granulomatous infiltration of the myocardium caused by sarcoidosis, which can produce conduction abnormalities, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, and heart failure.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, aggressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized by myocardial necrosis, mixed inflammatory infiltrates, and multinucleated giant cells; it commonly causes arrhythmias, heart failure, and conduction disease.

Chronic myocarditis with inflammatory ca.description: Persistent myocardial inflammation, often post-viral or autoimmune, that can lead to myocardial scarring, chamber enlargement, reduced cardiac function, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.

Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.normalized_text: Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome type 8)
Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.description: A rare autosomal-dominant calcium-channel disorder caused by pathogenic CACNA1C variants, classically p.Gly406Arg. It causes marked QT prolongation, functional 2:1 atrioventricular block, ventricular arrhythmias, and characteristic hand/foot syndactyly.

Atypical Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-relat.description: A CACNA1C-related disorder with severe QT prolongation and malignant arrhythmia risk but variable or incomplete extracardiac findings. Some affected individuals have less prominent syndactyly or neurodevelopmental manifestations than in classic Timothy syndrome.

Congenital long QT syndrome.description: An inherited cardiac ion-channel disorder characterized by delayed ventricular repolarization, QT prolongation, and increased risk of torsades de pointes, syncope, seizures, and sudden cardiac death. CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome is a specific subtype.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and FIP1L1-PDGFRA rearrangement (PDGFRA-associated chronic eosinophilic leukemia)
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by extreme persistent eosinophilia, often with hypercellular marrow and eosinophilic infiltration of tissues; it is commonly driven by a PDGFRA fusion and is typically highly responsive to imatinib.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A rare clonal myeloid neoplasm with sustained eosinophilia, evidence of abnormal myeloid proliferation and/or blasts or cytogenetic abnormalities, and exclusion of defining rearrangements such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A syndrome of persistent eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ injury after secondary causes and clonal myeloid neoplasms have been excluded. It may affect the skin, lungs, heart, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), BCR::ABL.normalized_text: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), BCR::ABL1-positive, with prominent eosinophilia
