Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), BCR::ABL.description: A BCR::ABL1-positive myeloproliferative neoplasm that usually causes marked leukocytosis with granulocytic proliferation, basophilia, splenomegaly, and sometimes eosinophilia. Molecular testing is required for diagnosis.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (diffuse astr.normalized_text: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (diffuse astrocytic glioma, WHO grade 4)
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (diffuse astr.description: An aggressive primary malignant glial tumor characterized by necrosis, vascular proliferation, infiltrative growth, marked surrounding edema, and frequent heterogeneous or ring enhancement. IDH-1 negativity with retained ATRX expression supports an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumor.

Glioblastoma with intratumoral hemorrhag.description: A glioblastoma may bleed spontaneously because of abnormal, fragile tumor blood vessels. Hemorrhage can obscure the underlying tumor on initial CT and may mimic a primary hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.

High-grade astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype.description: A malignant astrocytic neoplasm with high cellularity, mitotic activity, edema, contrast enhancement, and potential progression to or molecular classification as glioblastoma. In modern classification, many IDH-wildtype high-grade diffuse astrocytomas behave as glioblastoma when appropriate molecular features are present.

Solitary hemorrhagic brain metastasis.description: A metastatic cancer deposit in the brain can present as a well-circumscribed enhancing mass with extensive vasogenic edema and intratumoral hemorrhage. Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, and some lung cancers are particularly prone to hemorrhage.

Cerebral abscess.description: A focal intracranial infection that commonly appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with central fluid-like material and extensive surrounding vasogenic edema. Restricted diffusion and infectious clinical findings usually help distinguish it from a necrotic tumor.

Disseminated blastomycosis with vertebra.description: Blastomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by Blastomyces species. It commonly begins in the lungs and may disseminate to skin, bone, or the genitourinary tract. Bone involvement can cause destructive vertebral osteomyelitis and paraspinal soft-tissue masses.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with vertebr.description: Histoplasmosis is an infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, usually acquired through inhalation. It can leave calcified pulmonary granulomas and mediastinal lymph nodes and, rarely, disseminate to cause bone or vertebral infection.

Cryptococcal vertebral osteomyelitis.description: Cryptococcosis is an infection caused by Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii. It commonly affects the lungs and central nervous system but can rarely disseminate to bone, producing lytic vertebral lesions and soft-tissue masses.

Coccidioidomycosis with skeletal dissemi.description: Coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by Coccidioides species. Pulmonary infection may disseminate, particularly in susceptible individuals, causing osteomyelitis, vertebral destruction, and paraspinal abscesses.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Tuberculous spondylitis is vertebral infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically produces progressive vertebral destruction, disc-space involvement, and paraspinal or epidural abscesses; healed pulmonary tuberculosis can cause calcified lymph nodes.

Disseminated mucormycosis with pulmonary.normalized_text: Disseminated mucormycosis with pulmonary and necrotizing soft-tissue involvement
Disseminated mucormycosis with pulmonary.description: An invasive infection caused by Mucorales fungi that can involve the lungs and spread hematogenously to skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and fascia, causing rapidly progressive necrosis.

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with di.normalized_text: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with disseminated cutaneous/soft-tissue aspergillosis
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with di.description: A severe opportunistic Aspergillus infection that commonly affects the lungs and may disseminate to skin and soft tissues, producing necrotic lesions through vascular invasion.

Disseminated fusariosis.description: An opportunistic mold infection caused by Fusarium species that can cause pneumonia, fungemia, painful necrotic skin lesions, and deep soft-tissue infection, especially in immunocompromised patients.

Necrotizing fasciitis caused by an invas.normalized_text: Necrotizing fasciitis caused by an invasive fungal infection
Necrotizing fasciitis caused by an invas.description: A rapidly progressive infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue causing edema, erythema, tissue ischemia, and necrosis; fungi such as Mucorales, Aspergillus, or Fusarium can rarely cause this syndrome.

Congenital Zika virus infection (congeni.normalized_text: Congenital Zika virus infection (congenital Zika syndrome)
Congenital Zika virus infection (congeni.description: Fetal infection caused by maternal Zika virus infection during pregnancy, which can produce central nervous system abnormalities including ventriculomegaly, abnormal cortical development, calcifications, corpus callosum abnormalities, and microcephaly, although microcephaly may be absent prenatally.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A common congenital viral infection that can cause fetal brain injury, including ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, cortical malformations, microcephaly, hearing loss, and growth restriction.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: Transplacental infection with Toxoplasma gondii that can cause hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly, diffuse intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and neurologic impairment.

Fetal aqueductal stenosis or other obstr.normalized_text: Fetal aqueductal stenosis or other obstructive hydrocephalus
Fetal aqueductal stenosis or other obstr.description: Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow, often at the cerebral aqueduct, causing enlargement of the lateral ventricles and progressive hydrocephalus. It may be isolated or associated with genetic or structural brain abnormalities.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), comp.normalized_text: Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia
Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11), comp.description: An autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic SPG11 variants. It commonly produces progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness with a thin corpus callosum, cognitive impairment, peripheral neuropathy, and other complex neurologic features.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum (HSP-TCC)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin.description: A group of complicated hereditary spastic paraplegias characterized by progressive spastic paraparesis, cognitive impairment, and thinning of the corpus callosum. SPG11 is the most frequent genetic cause.

Spastic paraplegia type 15 (SPG15/Kjelli.description: An autosomal-recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by ZFYVE26 mutations, often associated with spastic paraparesis, cognitive impairment, a thin corpus callosum, white-matter disease, and sometimes retinal or extrapyramidal manifestations.

Cerebral palsy, spastic diplegic type.description: A nonprogressive motor disorder due to injury or abnormal development of the immature brain, commonly causing bilateral lower-extremity spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski signs.

Primary pulmonary artery sarcoma.description: A rare malignant tumor arising from the intima of the main pulmonary artery or proximal pulmonary arterial branches, often causing progressive obstruction of pulmonary blood flow and mimicking pulmonary embolism.

Pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma.description: A subtype of primary pulmonary artery sarcoma originating from mesenchymal cells of the pulmonary arterial intima. It commonly presents as an enlarging intraluminal mass with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and high PET metabolic activity.

Pulmonary embolism with chronic organize.normalized_text: Pulmonary embolism with chronic organized thrombus
Pulmonary embolism with chronic organize.description: Pulmonary embolism is obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombotic material. Chronic organized thrombus can appear as a persistent filling defect and may occasionally show limited enhancement, but typically has much lower metabolic activity than a sarcoma.

Cerebral nocardial abscess (nocardiosis).description: A focal brain infection caused by Nocardia species, aerobic branching filamentous bacteria that can produce multiloculated abscesses, particularly in immunocompromised patients but also occasionally in immunocompetent individuals.

Pyogenic bacterial brain abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within brain tissue caused by bacterial infection, commonly due to streptococci, staphylococci, anaerobes, gram-negative organisms, or Nocardia.

Cerebral phaeohyphomycosis due to Cladop.normalized_text: Cerebral phaeohyphomycosis due to Cladophialophora bantiana
Cerebral phaeohyphomycosis due to Cladop.description: A neurotropic dematiaceous fungal infection that can cause one or more brain abscesses, often with ring enhancement, edema, necrosis, and inflammatory tissue reaction.

Cerebral mucormycosis.description: An invasive fungal infection caused by Mucorales species that can invade blood vessels and produce cerebral infarction, hemorrhagic necrosis, or abscesses, usually in patients with diabetes or severe immunosuppression.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Toxoplasma gondii, typically producing multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions with edema in individuals with advanced HIV infection or other profound cellular immunosuppression.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often acquired by inhaling aerosolized contaminated freshwater from lakes, cottages, plumbing systems, hot tubs, or similar water sources.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.description: An acute infection of the lung parenchyma caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, or gram-negative organisms, producing focal or multifocal consolidation.

Acute viral pneumonia.description: A lower respiratory tract infection caused by respiratory viruses that can produce bilateral patchy ground-glass or air-space opacities, sometimes progressing rapidly.

Leptospirosis with pulmonary involvement.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira bacteria, acquired through contact with freshwater contaminated by animal urine. Severe disease can cause pulmonary infiltrates, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, and respiratory failure.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to.normalized_text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to environmental exposure
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis related to.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory lung reaction caused by inhaled environmental antigens, including mold, organic dust, or contaminated humidifier/hot-tub aerosols encountered in cottages or recreational settings.

COL13A1-related congenital myasthenic sy.description: A congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by deficiency of collagen XIII, a neuromuscular-junction extracellular matrix protein important for maturation and maintenance of pre- and postsynaptic structures. It can cause combined reductions in synaptic efficacy and endplate structural abnormalities.

Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congen.normalized_text: Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congenital myasthenic syndrome (for example, CHRNE-related CMS)
Acetylcholine receptor deficiency congen.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by reduced number or impaired function of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. It reduces the amplitude of miniature and evoked endplate responses.

DOK7-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by impaired Dok-7/MuSK signaling, leading to defective formation and maintenance of neuromuscular-junction postsynaptic architecture.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.description: An acquired presynaptic autoimmune disorder, usually mediated by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, causing reduced acetylcholine release and low quantal content.

Calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis.description: Kidney stones formed from calcium oxalate. Urine microscopy may show calcium oxalate crystals, including oval, dumbbell-shaped, or elongated "picket-fence" forms.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic ingestion of ethylene glycol can cause high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, and abundant calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals in urine.

Urinary tract infection with crystalluri.description: A urinary tract infection may coexist with urinary crystals, particularly when dehydration, urinary stasis, or altered urine pH is present. Some structures in the sediment could also represent cellular debris or microorganisms, although microscopy alone is not definitive.

Transient perivascular inflammation of t.normalized_text: Transient perivascular inflammation of the carotid artery (TIPIC syndrome, formerly carotidynia)
Transient perivascular inflammation of t.description: A benign, usually self-limited inflammatory condition characterized by focal perivascular soft-tissue inflammation around the carotid artery, often near the carotid bifurcation.

Carotid artery dissection.description: A tear in the arterial intima allowing blood to enter the vessel wall, producing mural hematoma, stenosis, pseudoaneurysm, or abnormal vessel-wall thickening. It can cause neck pain, headache, Horner syndrome, or cerebral ischemia.

Large-vessel vasculitis involving the ca.normalized_text: Large-vessel vasculitis involving the carotid artery
Large-vessel vasculitis involving the ca.description: Inflammatory disease of major arteries, such as Takayasu arteritis or giant-cell arteritis, which may produce arterial wall thickening, enhancement, narrowing, and surrounding inflammatory change.

Infectious carotid arteritis or deep nec.normalized_text: Infectious carotid arteritis or deep neck infection
Infectious carotid arteritis or deep nec.description: Bacterial infection involving tissues adjacent to the carotid sheath, sometimes causing inflammatory change around the carotid artery and potentially leading to thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, or abscess formation.

Carotid-space neoplasm or lymphadenopath.description: A mass in the carotid space, including metastatic lymphadenopathy, lymphoma, schwannoma, or paraganglioma, may displace or encase carotid vessels and mimic inflammatory soft-tissue thickening.

Whipple disease.description: A rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, most commonly involving the small intestine and producing malabsorption, lymphatic obstruction, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Intestinal biopsy typically shows lamina propria filled with foamy macrophages that are PAS-positive.

Celiac disease.description: An immune-mediated enteropathy caused by dietary gluten exposure in genetically susceptible individuals. It typically affects the proximal small intestine and causes villous injury, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the gastrointestinal tract, often the ileocecal region, with bowel-wall thickening and necrotic or enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Histology may demonstrate granulomatous inflammation.

Staphylococcus epidermidis infection or.normalized_text: Staphylococcus epidermidis infection or blood-culture contamination
Staphylococcus epidermidis infection or.description: A coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is normal skin flora but can cause catheter-, prosthetic-device-, and bloodstream-associated infections; it is also a common blood-culture contaminant.

Staphylococcus aureus infection.description: A virulent gram-positive coccus that commonly causes skin and soft-tissue infection, bacteremia, pneumonia, endocarditis, and invasive abscesses.

Micrococcus species infection or contami.description: Micrococcus species are aerobic gram-positive cocci found on skin and in the environment. They are usually culture contaminants but can occasionally cause opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients or those with intravascular devices.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Sarcoidosis with hepatic and splenic inv.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis with hepatic and splenic involvement
Sarcoidosis with hepatic and splenic inv.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that commonly affects the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes and can produce multiple small nodules in the liver and spleen.

Lymphoma with hepatic, splenic, and thor.normalized_text: Lymphoma with hepatic, splenic, and thoracic involvement
Lymphoma with hepatic, splenic, and thor.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that may involve lymph nodes, liver, spleen, lungs, and bone marrow; lymphoma lesions are often FDG-avid on PET imaging.

Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic a.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic and splenic granulomas
Disseminated tuberculosis with hepatic a.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can disseminate beyond the lungs and cause granulomatous nodules in the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and lungs.

Hepatic and splenic metastases from an o.normalized_text: Hepatic and splenic metastases from an occult malignancy
Hepatic and splenic metastases from an o.description: Metastatic cancer may cause multiple focal lesions in the liver and spleen and may be associated with thoracic lymphadenopathy or lung involvement.

Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary a.normalized_text: Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary artery (pulmonary artery sling)
Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary a.description: A congenital vascular anomaly in which the left pulmonary artery arises abnormally from the right pulmonary artery and may course between the trachea and esophagus, potentially causing airway compression.

Anomalous systemic arterial supply to th.normalized_text: Anomalous systemic arterial supply to the left lung (systemic-to-pulmonary arterial shunt)
Anomalous systemic arterial supply to th.description: A congenital vascular malformation in which a pulmonary arterial territory receives blood from an enlarged systemic artery, often arising from the aorta or one of its branches, causing enlarged abnormal thoracic vessels.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation.description: An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that bypasses the capillary bed, potentially producing enlarged feeding and draining vessels and right-to-left shunting.

Pulmonary artery aneurysm or focal pulmo.normalized_text: Pulmonary artery aneurysm or focal pulmonary artery dilatation
Pulmonary artery aneurysm or focal pulmo.description: Abnormal enlargement of a pulmonary artery segment, which may be congenital or secondary to pulmonary hypertension, vasculitis, infection, trauma, or a cardiac shunt.

Small bowel volvulus.description: Twisting of small bowel and its mesentery around the mesenteric vascular pedicle, which can cause closed-loop bowel obstruction and intestinal ischemia. The CT appearance may show a mesenteric 'whirl' sign.

Internal hernia with closed-loop small b.normalized_text: Internal hernia with closed-loop small bowel obstruction
Internal hernia with closed-loop small b.description: Protrusion of bowel through an internal peritoneal or mesenteric defect, potentially causing a closed-loop obstruction. CT can demonstrate clustered bowel loops, distorted mesenteric vessels, and a swirl/whirl configuration.

Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.normalized_text: Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation
Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.description: Congenital abnormal intestinal rotation can permit the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels. In adults it may present intermittently or acutely with bowel obstruction; CT may show a whirlpool appearance of mesenteric vessels.

Large left pneumothorax.description: Air in the left pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of the left lung.

Left tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening pneumothorax in which trapped pleural air raises intrathoracic pressure and can shift mediastinal structures and impair circulation.

Giant pulmonary bulla (bullous emphysema.description: A large air-filled emphysematous space within the lung that can mimic a pneumothorax on chest radiography.

Severe mitral regurgitation.description: Failure of the mitral valve to close fully during systole, causing backward flow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

Mitral valve prolapse with severe mitral.normalized_text: Mitral valve prolapse with severe mitral regurgitation
Mitral valve prolapse with severe mitral.description: Degenerative displacement of one or both mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole; severe prolapse can produce an eccentric mitral regurgitation jet.

Flail mitral leaflet or ruptured chordae.normalized_text: Flail mitral leaflet or ruptured chordae tendineae
Flail mitral leaflet or ruptured chordae.description: Loss of chordal support causes a mitral leaflet segment to move abnormally into the left atrium, often resulting in abrupt and severe mitral regurgitation.

Rheumatic mitral valve disease with mitr.normalized_text: Rheumatic mitral valve disease with mitral regurgitation
Rheumatic mitral valve disease with mitr.description: Chronic inflammatory scarring after rheumatic fever can thicken and deform the mitral valve, causing regurgitation, stenosis, or mixed mitral valve disease.

Infective endocarditis causing mitral re.description: Infection of the endocardial surface can damage mitral valve leaflets or chordae, producing acute or worsening mitral regurgitation.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.normalized_text: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis with epidural abscess
Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.description: Bacterial infection of adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervertebral disc that may extend into the epidural space and paraspinal soft tissues, producing neural compression.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) w.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with epidural and paraspinal abscess
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) w.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine causing vertebral destruction, disc-space involvement, paraspinal collections, and possible epidural extension with spinal canal compression.

Spinal epidural abscess secondary to inf.normalized_text: Spinal epidural abscess secondary to infectious spondylodiscitis
Spinal epidural abscess secondary to inf.description: A collection of infected material within the spinal epidural space, commonly arising from vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and capable of compressing the cauda equina or spinal nerve roots.

Spinal malignancy with epidural extensio.normalized_text: Spinal malignancy with epidural extension (metastatic disease or lymphoma)
Spinal malignancy with epidural extensio.description: Cancer involving vertebral marrow can cause vertebral destruction and epidural soft-tissue extension, leading to spinal canal compromise; however, prominent disc/endplate involvement favors infection over malignancy.

Angular cheilitis.description: Inflammation and fissuring at the corners of the mouth, often related to saliva maceration, Candida, Staphylococcus, irritation, nutritional deficiency, or poorly fitting dentures.

Impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, producing crusted erosions commonly around the mouth and nose.

Herpes simplex labialis.description: A recurrent herpes simplex virus infection of the lips or perioral skin that may cause painful grouped blisters, erosions, and crusting.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.description: A malignant tumor of keratinizing squamous cells that can occur on the lip or nearby skin and may present as a persistent crusted, ulcerated, or nonhealing lesion; regional lymph nodes can become enlarged if disease spreads.

Ecthyma.description: A deeper ulcerative form of impetigo caused by bacterial infection, characterized by adherent crust over a shallow ulcer and sometimes associated with nearby lymph-node enlargement.

NSAID-induced small-bowel diaphragm dise.description: A complication of chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use in which multiple thin, circumferential mucosal webs (diaphragms) form in the small intestine, causing multifocal strictures and intermittent obstruction.

Crohn disease with multifocal small-bowe.normalized_text: Crohn disease with multifocal small-bowel strictures
Crohn disease with multifocal small-bowe.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any gastrointestinal segment and may produce ulceration, inflammation, fibrosis, and obstructing strictures, particularly in the terminal ileum.

Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosin.description: A rare chronic disorder characterized by recurrent superficial small-bowel ulcers and multiple fibrotic strictures, often causing recurrent obstruction and iron-deficiency anemia.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can cause an annular constricting lesion, ulceration, bleeding, and bowel obstruction.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterial infection of the gastrointestinal tract, most often involving the ileocecal region, which may cause ulceration, mural thickening, strictures, adhesions, and bowel obstruction.

Dupuytren contracture.description: A fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that produces nodules and cords, progressively pulling one or more fingers into flexion.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon pulley system that can cause a finger to catch, lock, or remain flexed.

Post-traumatic flexion contracture of th.normalized_text: Post-traumatic flexion contracture of the finger
Post-traumatic flexion contracture of th.description: Persistent finger flexion caused by prior injury, scarring, tendon damage, or prolonged immobilization around the hand or finger joints.

Camptodactyly.description: A condition characterized by a flexion deformity of a finger, most commonly the little finger, due to soft-tissue and tendon imbalance.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic ne.description: A benign, self-limited inflammatory lymph-node disorder characterized by patchy necrosis with karyorrhectic debris, histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and typically few or no neutrophils. It commonly causes lymphadenopathy and may mimic lymphoma or infection.

Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae.description: A Bartonella infection causing regional lymphadenitis after inoculation from a cat scratch, bite, or flea exposure. Lymph nodes may show suppurative granulomatous inflammation with stellate necrosis and neutrophilic microabscesses.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of lymph nodes, usually producing chronic granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis. Cervical nodes are most common, but abdominal, pelvic, and inguinal nodes may be involved.

Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated.description: Autoimmune lymph-node inflammation associated with systemic lupus erythematosus that can closely resemble Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically. It may show necrosis, hematoxylin bodies, plasma cells, and vasculitic changes.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Pleural epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.description: A rare malignant vascular tumor arising from pleura or lung, characterized histologically by epithelioid endothelial cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles in a myxohyaline stroma. It can resemble mesothelioma on imaging.

Malignant pleural mesothelioma.description: An aggressive cancer of pleural mesothelial cells, often associated with asbestos exposure, that commonly causes unilateral pleural effusion, diffuse nodular pleural thickening, and encasement of the lung.

Metastatic pleural adenocarcinoma.description: Metastatic spread of adenocarcinoma, commonly from lung, breast, ovary, gastrointestinal tract, or other primary sites, can involve the pleura and produce malignant pleural effusion and nodular pleural thickening.

Primary splenic angiosarcoma.description: A rare, aggressive malignant vascular tumor arising from splenic endothelial cells. It often presents as a solitary heterogeneous splenic mass and may show pleomorphic malignant cells with vascular/endothelial immunostaining.

Splenic hemangioma.description: A benign vascular tumor of the spleen and one of the most common benign splenic lesions. It may appear as a focal splenic mass, although cytology generally lacks marked malignant atypia.

Littoral cell angioma.description: An uncommon vascular splenic neoplasm arising from littoral cells lining splenic red-pulp sinuses. It can produce splenic nodules or splenomegaly and may express endothelial and histiocytic markers.

Primary splenic lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the spleen, which can present as a solitary splenic mass or diffuse splenic enlargement. Large-cell lymphoma may show atypical large cells on fine-needle aspiration.

Inflammatory pseudotumor-like follicular.normalized_text: Inflammatory pseudotumor-like follicular dendritic cell tumor of the spleen
Inflammatory pseudotumor-like follicular.description: A rare splenic neoplasm composed of spindle to oval follicular dendritic cells with a prominent inflammatory background, frequently associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

Ebstein anomaly.description: A congenital malformation of the tricuspid valve characterized by apical displacement of the valve leaflets, atrialization of part of the right ventricle, right-atrial enlargement, and often significant tricuspid regurgitation.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.description: A cardiac pre-excitation syndrome caused by an accessory atrioventricular conduction pathway, producing early ventricular activation and predisposing to supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

Severe tricuspid regurgitation secondary.normalized_text: Severe tricuspid regurgitation secondary to Ebstein anomaly
Severe tricuspid regurgitation secondary.description: In Ebstein anomaly, malformed and displaced tricuspid valve leaflets may fail to coapt, allowing substantial backward flow from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole.

Congenital right-sided heart disease wit.normalized_text: Congenital right-sided heart disease with atrialized right ventricle
Congenital right-sided heart disease wit.description: A congenital structural disorder involving abnormal tricuspid valve development and functional separation of the right ventricle into an atrialized proximal segment and a functional distal chamber; this pattern is most characteristic of Ebstein anomaly.

Acute ischemic cerebral infarction.description: An acute stroke caused by reduced blood flow to brain tissue, commonly due to arterial occlusion or embolism. Diffusion-weighted MRI typically shows restricted diffusion with low ADC signal in the early phase.

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A mitochondrial disorder that can cause recurrent stroke-like brain lesions, often involving the temporal, parietal, or occipital cortex. Lesions may not follow a single arterial vascular territory and may occur despite normal angiography.

Peri-ictal MRI abnormality due to focal.normalized_text: Peri-ictal MRI abnormality due to focal seizure or status epilepticus
Peri-ictal MRI abnormality due to focal.description: Prolonged focal seizures can produce transient cortical diffusion restriction and swelling on MRI, sometimes mimicking an acute infarct. Such abnormalities may occur without arterial occlusion and may improve or migrate on follow-up imaging.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing aortic wall thickening, stenosis, occlusion, aneurysmal change, renal artery involvement, and aortic regurgitation.

Giant cell arteritis with aortitis.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries that can involve the thoracic and abdominal aorta, producing aortitis, aneurysm, stenosis, and occasionally aortic valve regurgitation.

Infectious aortitis or mycotic aortic an.normalized_text: Infectious aortitis or mycotic aortic aneurysm
Infectious aortitis or mycotic aortic an.description: Infection of the aortic wall, usually bacterial, causing intense inflammation, wall destruction, pseudoaneurysm or aneurysm formation, and potentially valvular involvement or regurgitation.

Behçet disease with aortic vasculitis.description: A systemic inflammatory vasculitis that can affect arteries and veins of all sizes; arterial involvement may cause aortitis, aneurysms, pseudoaneurysms, thrombosis, and aortic valve regurgitation.

IgG4-related aortitis/periaortitis.description: A fibroinflammatory immune-mediated disorder that can involve the aorta and its branches, causing aortic wall thickening, periaortic soft tissue, aneurysm formation, stenosis, and occasionally involvement of other organs.

Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvu.description: A congenital abnormal rotation/fixation of the bowel that can allow the small intestine and mesentery to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, producing the CT whirlpool sign and potentially causing bowel obstruction or ischemia.

Primary small-bowel volvulus.description: Twisting of a segment of small bowel and its mesentery around the mesenteric vascular pedicle, which may cause closed-loop obstruction and compromise bowel blood supply.

Internal hernia with mesenteric volvulus.description: Herniation of small bowel through a mesenteric or peritoneal defect can twist the mesentery, creating a whirlpool appearance and causing intermittent or acute small-bowel obstruction.

Primary epithelial (epidermoid) splenic.description: A benign congenital nonparasitic splenic cyst, often large and solitary, with internal echoes from proteinaceous or hemorrhagic material.

Splenic pseudocyst.description: A nonparasitic splenic cyst, commonly occurring after prior trauma, hemorrhage, or infection; it may contain debris, septations, calcification, or internal echoes.

Splenic hydatid cyst.description: A parasitic cyst caused by Echinococcus infection that can involve the spleen and may appear as a large cyst with internal debris, daughter cysts, or detached membranes.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized infection within the spleen that may form a complex fluid collection with internal debris, septations, and occasionally gas.

Splenic lymphangioma.description: A benign congenital malformation of splenic lymphatic vessels that may present as one or more cystic lesions, often multiloculated with thin septations.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome caused by a deletion of chromosome 11p11.2, typically involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple osteochondromas/exostoses, enlarged parietal foramina, craniofacial abnormalities, and frequently developmental delay.

Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, most often due to pathogenic variants or deletions involving EXT1 or EXT2, causing multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near metaphyses of long bones.

Isolated enlarged parietal foramina.description: A skull ossification disorder caused most commonly by pathogenic variants involving ALX4 or MSX2, producing persistent enlarged openings in the parietal bones near the sagittal suture.

Cleidocranial dysplasia.description: A skeletal dysplasia usually caused by RUNX2 pathogenic variants, characterized by delayed closure of cranial sutures and fontanelles, clavicular hypoplasia, dental abnormalities, and delayed ossification.

Crusted scabies (Norwegian scabies).description: A severe, highly contagious infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei mites, often causing extensive crusting, hyperkeratosis, erosions, and numerous mites in the superficial epidermis.

Classic scabies.description: A pruritic skin infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, usually producing papules, burrows, excoriations, and eczematous lesions; mites can be identified in the stratum corneum.

Pediculosis corporis (body lice infestat.description: Infestation by body lice that causes severe itching and excoriated papules or eczematous skin lesions, typically affecting the trunk and areas in contact with clothing seams.

Impetiginized dermatitis or secondary ba.normalized_text: Impetiginized dermatitis or secondary bacterial skin infection
Impetiginized dermatitis or secondary ba.description: A bacterial superinfection, commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, occurring in disrupted skin and producing crusting, erosions, ulceration, and inflammation.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.description: An immune-complex-mediated glomerular disease characterized by mesangial proliferation, lobular accentuation of the glomerulus, and thickening or duplication of capillary walls.

Diabetic nephropathy with nodular glomer.description: Chronic diabetic kidney disease causing mesangial matrix expansion, glomerular basement-membrane thickening, and sometimes nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.

Lupus nephritis, proliferative form (cla.normalized_text: Lupus nephritis, proliferative form (class III or IV)
Lupus nephritis, proliferative form (cla.description: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis caused by systemic lupus erythematosus, often producing marked mesangial and endocapillary proliferation with capillary-wall immune deposits.

IgA nephropathy / IgA vasculitis-associa.description: An immune-complex glomerular disease with predominantly mesangial IgA deposition, often causing mesangial proliferation and variable glomerular scarring.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disease causing bile-duct wall thickening and strictures, characterized by dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with increased IgG4-positive plasma cells. It may occur with or without autoimmune pancreatitis.

Autoimmune pancreatitis type 1 with asso.normalized_text: Autoimmune pancreatitis type 1 with associated IgG4-related cholangitis
Autoimmune pancreatitis type 1 with asso.description: Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related disease and can cause pancreatic inflammation, pancreatic enlargement, and associated stricturing of the bile ducts.

Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor.description: A malignant tumor arising from the bile-duct epithelium at the hepatic hilum, typically producing obstruction of the right and left hepatic ducts and upstream biliary dilatation.
